arguments.name: Partner-channel price and service-bundle pilot
arguments.method: Run a limited online and retail-partner pilot in two German-speaking markets with a compact prosumer machine. Randomise listing to three arms: (a) machine at a premium price (proposed: 25% above a comparable prosumer machine), (b) same machine with a 3-year service plan included, (c) same machine at the premium price with no service option. Measure click-to-purchase conversion and service-plan take-up. Price points and arms are proposed, not observed.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm across partner product pages, roughly 9,000 total, over 8 weeks
arguments.measure: Purchase conversion rate per arm; share of buyers taking the service plan; stated willingness to pay from a short post-purchase or exit survey

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm (a) converts at a rate within 20% of a comparable prosumer baseline, and arm (c) shows no meaningful drop versus (a); premium price holds without a service bundle.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm (b) converts clearly higher than arm (a) and (c), and service-plan take-up exceeds 15% of buyers; price premium alone converts poorly.

arguments.decision_rule: Proceed to a full partner-channel launch only if arm (a) conversion is at least 70% of the comparable prosumer baseline AND arm (a) partner margin still gives Franke at least its professional unit gross margin (estimate to be confirmed with finance). If arm (b) beats (a) by 25% or more with service take-up above 15%, favour a service-bundled model instead. If neither threshold is met, do not invest beyond the pilot.

X1.name: Feature-bundle vs service-attach demand test (Japan, proposed)
X1.method: Two-arm stated-preference and interest test. Arm A: a web survey plus conjoint choice of household fridges, with automatic ice as an attribute at several price points. Arm B: a refundable pre-order page for a countertop ice unit, with and without a bundled annual service plan at the same price. In parallel, structured interviews with refrigerator makers and appliance dealers in Japan to test OEM appetite for an outside ice module (T1), and dealer willingness to route residential sales to a service contract (T2).
X1.sample: Proposed: about 400 Japanese households who have bought or plan to buy a fridge in the next 12 months (online panel, quota-matched by region); 8 to 10 interviews with refrigerator makers and dealers. All sample sizes are estimates for this exercise.
X1.measure: Arm A: willingness to pay for automatic ice as a share of fridge choice and implied EUR premium. Arm B: pre-order conversion with vs without service plan, and service-plan take-up rate. Interviews: number of OEMs willing to hold a supplier discussion or RFQ.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Automatic ice carries a measurable premium in the conjoint and OEM interviews show several makers willing to open a supplier discussion; service plan adds little to pre-order conversion because ice is valued as a fridge feature.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Service plan lifts pre-order conversion materially over no-plan, service take-up is high among buyers who cite repair or installation worry, and dealers will route residential sales to a service contract; OEM interest in ice modules is low or absent.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: favour T1 if at least 3 of 8 to 10 OEMs agree to a supplier discussion AND automatic ice shows at least a 10% premium in the conjoint. Favour T2 if the service-plan pre-order uplift is at least 15 percentage points over no-plan AND at least 3 dealers commit to routing. If neither threshold is met, or both are, treat the result as unresolved and do not commit more than the test budget. Thresholds are proposed, not validated.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product or partnership now. Keep the commercial focus as the default (alternative A). Before any decision, run test X1 as a proposed EUR 20,000, 12-week check of two consumer routes: OEM ice-module supply (T1) and a service-attached residential offer (T2). Treat the thresholds as proposed, not validated.
final.target_customer: Not yet determined. Candidate segments are Japanese households buying a fridge or countertop ice unit (T1 and T2 both point here), but no source establishes demand in this segment.
final.value_proposition: Unproven. A candidate is an automatic-ice module for refrigerator makers (T1) or a service contract on residential ice units (T2). Neither has evidence of willingness to pay.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed): conjoint and pre-order test with about 400 Japanese households, plus 8 to 10 interviews with refrigerator makers and dealers. Ask Hoshizaki for its own residential sales and service data, which is not public.
final.uncertainty: High. The company profile describes only commercial kitchen equipment, so no public source shows a household product or residential service. Renub's household claim is undated and has no stated method. The GMI excerpt suggests residential ice enters through standalone countertop units, which weakens T1. I found no source for Hoshizaki's direct-channel reach to individual buyers, consumer share of sales, distributor terms or margins; these are not public. Both theories are unverified.

frame.objective: Decide whether Hoshizaki should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its commercial ice machines and kitchen equipment, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is to find a use case where Hoshizaki's existing capabilities (ice making, refrigeration, direct sales and service) earn a return a consumer will pay for, without damaging its commercial franchise.

D. Different customer group: serve small commercial or semi-professional users (home bars, cafes, small offices, caterers) with a light proposition
E. Service-led proposition: sell maintenance, filtration, or ice-quality subscriptions to existing or new users rather than hardware
F. Adjacent category via partner: license the brand or technology to a consumer appliance maker, capturing royalty without consumer channel risk

T1.claim: Consumers in homes will pay a premium for chewable nugget-style ice from a compact countertop machine, because the ice texture is a craving they cannot otherwise satisfy. A nugget-ice appliance sold through retail or online to home-bar and kitchen buyers could earn premium hardware margins plus repeat filter and cleaning revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home consumers who crave chewable ice; Hoshizaki (or its Scotsman brand) as the hardware maker and seller of consumables
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Chewable ice is a sensory preference that commercial dispensers serve but home freezers cannot. Once a consumer can buy the texture at home, the craving becomes a purchase motive, similar to the way home espresso machines turned a café habit into a household appliance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Hardware sales at a premium price point, then recurring revenue from filters, descaling products and extended warranties, sold through channels Hoshizaki does not yet control, or through a partner's retail network.
assumptions: The craving for nugget ice is strong and widespread enough to justify a premium price in the home market
Households have counter or under-counter space and will accept a noisy, water-connected appliance
A consumer product can be sold through retail or online without the direct service network
Hoshizaki's existing consumer-scale nugget technology can be packaged for home use at acceptable cost
predictions: In a stated-preference or pre-order test, a meaningful share of target buyers (for example 5 to 10 percent, proposed threshold) will show purchase intent at a price above a standard home ice maker
Purchase intent concentrates in households that already buy chewable ice or cite it as a reason for visiting restaurants
Demand falls sharply if the price is set near that of a standard freezer-tray ice maker
T1.first_claim: Consumers in homes will pay a premium for chewable nugget-style ice from a compact countertop machine, because the ice texture is a craving they cannot otherwise satisfy. A nugget-ice appliance sold through retail or online to home-bar and kitchen buyers could earn premium hardware margins plus repeat filter and cleaning revenue.

T2.claim: The binding constraint on a consumer ice product is not the product but after-sales upkeep. Households avoid countertop ice machines because cleaning, descaling, filter changes and repairs fall on them. A maker with an existing installed base and a field service network could capture value by selling a maintenance and water-quality service that makes ownership easy, with hardware as the entry point.
T2.who_benefits: Households that want clean ice without maintenance chores; Hoshizaki as the operator of the service and filter revenue stream
T2.why_behaviour_changes: People buy appliances they expect to run without attention. Ice machines have a reputation for slime, scale and noise, so the purchase decision turns on whether upkeep is handled. A bundled service removes the reason to decline the purchase, even when the buyer would not pay for the machine alone.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Service contracts and consumables (filters, cleaning kits) on an installed base, possibly sold to existing commercial customers' households or through a partner, with the hardware sold at close to cost.
assumptions: Upkeep, not the ice itself, is the main barrier to buying a home ice machine
Households will pay a recurring fee for service, and the fee exceeds the cost of providing it
Hoshizaki's existing service network and parts logistics can extend to residential addresses at acceptable cost
Commercial customers' staff or contacts can serve as a referral route to home buyers
predictions: In a stated-choice test, adding a bundled maintenance plan raises purchase intent more than an equivalent cut in hardware price
Buyers who decline the machine cite cleaning or maintenance as the main reason more often than price or counter space
Willingness to pay for maintenance is highest among households that already use a separate water-filtering or appliance-service plan
T2.first_claim: The binding constraint on a consumer ice product is not the product but after-sales upkeep. Households avoid countertop ice machines because cleaning, descaling, filter changes and repairs fall on them. A maker with an existing installed base and a field service network could capture value by selling a maintenance and water-quality service that makes ownership easy, with hardware as the entry point.

assessments.quote: For the first time, consumers can satisfy their cravings for this delicious ice in the convenience of their own homes.
assessments.does_not_show: This is the maker's own marketing claim from a 2011 press release. It does not show that a craving exists in a large enough group, that households bought the product, what they paid, or whether sales held up. It also does not show that Scotsman belongs to Hoshizaki: my sources do not establish that link, so I cannot treat this as Hoshizaki's own consumer product.

assessments.quote: Hoshizaki Alliance is a group of independent companies that manufacture and market products for the food service industry, including ice machines, refrigerators, freezers, prep tables, display cases, and dispensers.

It says nothing about residential customers, household maintenance, service plans or whether any residential service network exists. It cannot tell me whether maintenance is a real barrier for home buyers, or whether Hoshizaki could serve homes at acceptable cost.

X1.name: Craving versus upkeep: priced landing-page and stated-choice test with home-bar and kitchen households
X1.method: Online randomised stated-choice test. Participants see a countertop nugget-ice machine concept with price and feature variants: (a) hardware only at a premium price, (b) hardware at a lower price, (c) same hardware with a bundled cleaning, descaling and filter service plan. Screen first for households that already buy chewable ice or cite it as a reason to visit restaurants, and for a general household group. Follow with a refundable deposit pre-order on a landing page for the best-performing variant, if intent clears the threshold.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 600 respondents across two screened groups (craving-screened and general), roughly 300 each, recruited through an online panel. Estimated panel cost and landing-page traffic fit within the EUR 20,000 budget.
X1.measure: Primary: share choosing a purchase or deposit in each variant, by screen group. Secondary: stated reason for declining (price, counter space, upkeep, noise), and willingness to pay for the service plan.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Craving-screened households show the highest purchase intent for hardware, and a lower hardware price raises intent more than adding a service plan. The gap between craving and general groups is large.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Adding the service plan raises intent more than a comparable hardware price cut, and upkeep is the most frequently cited reason for declining in the general group, with craving-screened households not differing much from it.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the service-plan variant raises deposit or purchase intent by at least 5 percentage points more than the hardware price cut, and upkeep is the leading stated decline reason, favour T2 and pursue a service-led test. If the craving-screened group shows at least 8 percent deposit or purchase intent at the premium hardware price, and the price cut beats the service plan, favour T1 and test a consumer hardware prototype. If neither threshold is met, or the results are within 3 points of each other, decline further investment and treat the consumer opportunity as unproven. These thresholds are proposed, not derived from data.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product or home channel now. Run the proposed stated-choice and pre-order test (X1) first, at an estimated EUR 18,000 and 10 weeks, and decide from its thresholds. My sources do not show that Hoshizaki has consumer demand, a consumer product, or a residential service network. The only consumer evidence is a 2011 US Scotsman press release asserting a craving for nugget ice at home. My sources do not establish that Scotsman belongs to Hoshizaki, and Hoshizaki's profile lists commercial kitchen appliances only.
final.target_customer: Not yet chosen. Candidates to test: craving-screened households (already buy chewable ice or cite it when visiting restaurants) and general households, where upkeep may be the main barrier.
final.value_proposition: Untested. A (T1): compact countertop chewable-ice machine at a premium price. B (T2): bundled cleaning, descaling and filter service, with hardware as the entry point.
final.next_action: Run test X1: stated-choice variants (premium hardware, cheaper hardware, hardware plus service) across craving-screened and general households, then a deposit pre-order for the best variant. Thresholds: service beats price cut by 5+ points with upkeep leading decline reasons favours T2; craving-screened intent of 8%+ at premium price favours T1; otherwise treat as unproven. Seek the company's consumer sales history and residential service data.
final.uncertainty: High. The only demand claim is one 2011 company press release, not independent evidence of demand, price, volume or margin. No independent market size, competitor data, cost data or residential service evidence found. Scotsman-Hoshizaki link unverified. T2 has no supporting evidence. My challenge search for T1 returned only the same company material, which is not a real test. Test parameters and thresholds are my proposals, not observed figures.
would_change_if: Independent data showing residential countertop ice machine sales are small or falling (weakens T1)
Evidence the Scotsman consumer line is Hoshizaki's and underperformed or was discontinued
X1 showing service beats price cut by 5+ points with upkeep as main decline reason (moves favour to T2)
X1 showing 8%+ craving-screened intent at premium price (supports T1 and a prototype)
Evidence of an existing residential customer base for Hoshizaki units (cheaper service route)
Non-public contract terms, such as distributor exclusivity, that rule out a consumer channel

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Chewable ice is a sensory preference that commercial dispensers serve but home freezers cannot. Once a consumer can buy the texture at home, the craving becomes a purchase motive, similar to the way home espresso machines turned a café habit into a household appliance.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Hardware sales at a premium price point, then recurring revenue from filters, descaling products and extended warranties, sold through channels Hoshizaki does not yet control, or through a partner's retail network.

arguments.claim: The binding constraint on a consumer ice product is not the product but after-sales upkeep. arguments.why_behaviour_changes: People buy appliances they expect to run without attention. arguments.name: Craving versus upkeep: priced landing-page and stated-choice test with home-bar and kitchen households
arguments.method: Online randomised stated-choice test. Participants see a countertop nugget-ice machine concept with price and feature variants: (a) hardware only at a premium price, (b) hardware at a lower price, (c) same hardware with a bundled cleaning, descaling and filter service plan. Screen first for households that already buy chewable ice or cite it as a reason to visit restaurants, and for a general household group. Follow with a refundable deposit pre-order on a landing page for the best-performing variant, if intent clears the threshold.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 600 respondents across two screened groups (craving-screened and general), roughly 300 each, recruited through an online panel. Estimated panel cost and landing-page traffic fit within the EUR 20,000 budget.
arguments.measure: Primary: share choosing a purchase or deposit in each variant, by screen group. Secondary: stated reason for declining (price, counter space, upkeep, noise), and willingness to pay for the service plan.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Craving-screened households show the highest purchase intent for hardware, and a lower hardware price raises intent more than adding a service plan. The gap between craving and general groups is large.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Adding the service plan raises intent more than a comparable hardware price cut, and upkeep is the most frequently cited reason for declining in the general group, with craving-screened households not differing much from it.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the service-plan variant raises deposit or purchase intent by at least 5 percentage points more than the hardware price cut, and upkeep is the leading stated decline reason, favour T2 and pursue a service-led test. If the craving-screened group shows at least 8 percent deposit or purchase intent at the premium hardware price, and the price cut beats the service plan, favour T1 and test a consumer hardware prototype. If neither threshold is met, or the results are within 3 points of each other, decline further investment and treat the consumer opportunity as unproven. These thresholds are proposed, not derived from data.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to developing a consumer product yet. Run the proposed stated-choice test (X1) before any product or channel investment. I favour T1 only because it is the one theory with any supporting evidence, a single company assertion, and my challenge search found nothing against it. That is weak support, not a finding that consumer demand exists.

Do not commit to a consumer product or home channel now. Run the proposed stated-choice and pre-order test (X1) first, at an estimated EUR 18,000 and 10 weeks, and decide from its thresholds. What I found does not show that Hoshizaki has consumer demand, a consumer product, or a residential service network. The only consumer evidence I read is a 2011 US press release from Scotsman, which asserts a craving for nugget ice at home and describes a 15-inch consumer ice machine category created about 40 years earlier. My sources do not establish that Scotsman belongs to Hoshizaki. Hoshizaki's own profile lists commercial kitchen appliances only.
arguments.target_customer: Not yet chosen. Candidate groups to test are households that already buy chewable ice or cite it as a reason to visit restaurants (craving-screened), and general households, where upkeep may be the main barrier.
arguments.value_proposition: Untested. Candidate A (T1): a compact countertop chewable-ice machine at a premium price. Candidate B (T2): a bundled cleaning, descaling and filter service that makes a home ice machine easy to own, with hardware as the entry point.
arguments.next_action: Run test X1: randomised stated-choice variants (hardware premium, hardware price cut, hardware plus service plan) across craving-screened and general households, with a deposit pre-order for the best variant. Use the proposed thresholds: service plan beats price cut by at least 5 points with upkeep leading decline reasons favours T2; craving-screened deposit or purchase intent of at least 8 percent at premium price favours T1; otherwise treat the consumer opportunity as unproven. Also seek the company's own consumer sales history, subsidiary structure and any residential service data, which are not in my sources.
arguments.uncertainty: High. The only demand-related claim is a single 2011 company press release, which is not independent evidence of demand, price, volume or margin. I found no independent market size, no competitor sales data, no cost data and no evidence on whether Hoshizaki's service network can reach homes. The Scotsman-Hoshizaki link is unverified. T2 has no supporting evidence at all, and my challenge search for T1 returned only the same company material, which is not a real test. Both theories are uncertain. Test parameters, sample and thresholds are my proposals, not observed figures.

Test X1 showing at least 8 percent craving-screened intent at premium price, which would support T1 and justify a prototype
Discovery of residential service demand or an existing residential customer base for Hoshizaki units, which would make the service-led route cheaper to test

X1.name: Parallel demand test: stand-alone premium ice unit vs ice-module OEM interest
X1.method: Two low-cost parallel probes over 12 weeks. (a) Consumer probe: online concept page for a compact commercial-grade home ice maker with a refundable deposit at a proposed price, plus a short survey on ice use and purchase reasons, targeted at Japanese households that entertain at home. (b) OEM probe: structured outreach to refrigerator makers and appliance component buyers asking for a non-binding engineering-quote request for an external ice module, using a one-page spec.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 1,500 unique visitors from paid and owned channels in Japan for the consumer probe; about 25 refrigerator or appliance-component buyers contacted for the OEM probe (estimated list size, to be confirmed).
X1.measure: Consumer: deposit conversion rate at the proposed price and survey share ranking ice quality/speed above price. OEM: number of qualified buyers who request a quote or technical meeting within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Deposit conversion at a premium price is meaningful, and ice quality/speed ranks above price in purchase reasons; OEM interest is low because the value is in the stand-alone brand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer deposit conversion is low or price-sensitive, while several OEM buyers request quotes and technical meetings.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: pursue T1 further only if deposit conversion is at or above 3% of unique visitors AND at least 60% of survey respondents rank ice quality or speed above price. Pursue T2 further only if at least 3 qualified OEM buyers request a quote or technical meeting within 12 weeks. If neither threshold is met, do not invest in a product or module program and keep focus on existing commercial lines. If both are met, run a second round to compare.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer product or new consumer channel now. Keep the commercial focus. Run the proposed low-cost test (X1) to decide between a stand-alone premium home ice unit (T1) and an OEM ice-module route (T2). Public evidence found so far does not justify either investment.
final.target_customer: Undetermined. Candidates: Japanese households that entertain at home (T1) and refrigerator or appliance-component makers (T2). Neither is established by evidence.
final.value_proposition: Undetermined. Under T1, commercial-grade ice quality and speed in a compact home unit. Under T2, an ice-making module sold to refrigerator makers at component margin.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, about EUR 15,000 over 12 weeks, estimated). First confirm the OEM contact list and whether Hoshizaki already sells any consumer or home products; the sources read did not establish this.
final.uncertainty: High. Hoshizaki's consumer reach is unestablished; its pages describe a food-service maker and I found no consumer line. The Renub fridge-feature summary (undated, secondary) fits both theories and tests neither. No data on willingness to pay, channel economics, OEM sourcing or margins. The search for contrary evidence on T2 found nothing direct, which is weak support, not proof. Test figures are my proposals.

The public evidence I found does not yet justify either investment.
arguments.target_customer: Undetermined. Candidates are Japanese households that entertain at home (T1) and refrigerator or appliance-component makers (T2). Neither is established by evidence.
arguments.value_proposition: Undetermined. Under T1, commercial-grade ice quality and speed in a compact home unit. Under T2, a proven ice-making module sold to refrigerator makers at component margin.
arguments.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, about EUR 15,000 over 12 weeks, estimated). Before running it, confirm the OEM contact list and whether Hoshizaki already sells any consumer or home products; I could not establish this from the sources read.
arguments.uncertainty: High. (1) I could not establish how far Hoshizaki reaches individual buyers; the company's own pages describe it as a food-service manufacturer, and I found no consumer product line in the sources. (2) Renub's summary of Japanese fridge features (undated, secondary, no method) lists automatic ice makers among features valued, which fits both theories and tests neither. (3) No evidence on willingness to pay, consumer channel economics, refrigerator-maker sourcing practices, margins or distribution contracts; these are likely non-public. (4) The challenge search for evidence against T2 returned no direct contrary source, which is weak evidence in T2's favour, not proof. (5) Hoshizaki's FY2025 presentation is a company claim about overseas demand for ice machines, refrigerators and dispensers, not consumer demand. (6) All numbers in the test (sample, budget, threshold, weeks) are my proposals, not observed facts.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer product yet. Favour a cheap pre-order test of a premium nugget-texture compact unit before any redesign. If the test fails the decision rule, stay commercial and pursue service or OEM options.

frame.objective: Decide whether Hoshizaki should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home ice, home beverage or kitchen appliances for individual buyers), or stay commercial-only. Identify the evidence that would justify the investment, and find out how far Hoshizaki already reaches individual buyers before assuming it does not.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Financial and contractual detail may not be public; note what could not be found
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget is 8 searches (7 left), so evidence must be targeted
Must not assume Hoshizaki's current consumer reach; verify it first
alternatives: A. No expansion: remain a commercial ice machine, refrigeration and dispenser maker sold through direct sales and service networks
B. Product redesign: adapt an existing commercial line (for example a compact ice maker) for home or small-office use, sold through existing channels
C. Different route to buyers: sell a consumer range through retail, online or appliance-brand partnerships, with Hoshizaki's brand in the background
D. Different customer group: serve a specific segment such as small cafés, home-based food businesses or premium home bar owners
E. Service-led or connected proposition: sell maintenance, filters, replenishment or monitoring to existing installed-base owners, with no new consumer hardware
F. Licensing or OEM supply: supply core ice-making or compressor modules to consumer appliance brands and capture value without owning the consumer relationship

T1.claim: Some home buyers want a specific ice texture (chewable nugget ice) that standard fridge ice does not provide, so a compact consumer machine that makes that ice can earn a premium price and repeat consumable sales.
T1.who_benefits: Home buyers who value nugget or chewable ice; the manufacturer that owns the design, brand and consumable supply.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who already know and want nugget ice from restaurants or drinks outlets have a strong texture preference and will pay for a home version rather than go without.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium unit price for a 15-inch consumer machine sold through appliance retail or direct online, plus filters or service revenue from owners.
assumptions: A meaningful pool of households wants nugget ice enough to buy a dedicated machine
The product can be made at a cost that supports a premium price
Owners keep using the machine and replace filters or parts
predictions: Units sell mainly to buyers who already report nugget ice as a preference
Purchase price holds above standard compact ice makers
Filter or service attach rate is high among owners
T1.first_claim: Some home buyers want a specific ice texture (chewable nugget ice) that standard fridge ice does not provide, so a compact consumer machine that makes that ice can earn a premium price and repeat consumable sales.

T2.claim: Consumer ice machines are a low-frequency, low-margin niche in which the manufacturer's real earnings come from the commercial installed base and its service contracts, so a consumer range adds little value unless it is sold through an existing channel with little extra cost.
T2.who_benefits: The commercial operator and service network that already holds the customer relationship; consumer buyers gain little from a Hoshizaki-branded product over cheaper rivals.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers buy a home ice maker occasionally and compare on price and reliability, not on the maker's commercial reputation, so brand premium is weak and the purchase is a one-off.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Value is captured through commercial sales, service contracts and parts, not consumer units. A consumer line is justified only if it reuses existing production and channels at near-zero marginal cost.
assumptions: Consumer buyers buy on price and do not pay a brand premium for commercial pedigree
Consumer units have low replacement frequency
Commercial service revenue exceeds what a consumer line could earn
predictions: Consumer models sell at prices close to the category average, not at a premium
Consumer units have little or no attached service or filter revenue
The manufacturer's commercial margins are not improved by a consumer line

X1.name: Premium pre-order smoke test for a compact nugget-texture home ice maker
X1.method: Single-market online pre-order test with a landing page showing a compact home ice maker concept, using a neutral brand placeholder so the test does not rely on Hoshizaki or Scotsman identity. Two price cells are shown at random: a premium price and a category-average price (both proposed, to be set from a competitor price scan first). The page asks visitors a short preference question about ice texture and whether they have bought a home ice maker before. Pre-orders are refundable deposits, not sales. Traffic is bought through paid search and social targeting in one country.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 unique visitors per price cell, targeted at adults who own a fridge and have searched for ice or drinks-at-home terms. Estimated cost is paid traffic plus page build and survey tool, within EUR 20,000.
X1.measure: Pre-order conversion rate per price cell; share of pre-orders that state a nugget or chewable texture preference; share of visitors who chose the premium cell and completed the texture question; cost per pre-order.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Premium cell converts at a rate close to the average cell, and a clearly higher share of pre-orders cite nugget or chewable texture as the reason, so the texture preference is the driver rather than price tolerance alone.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium cell converts well below the average cell, and texture preference is cited rarely, so buyers respond to price and reliability rather than a specific ice experience.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: proceed to a costed pilot only if the premium cell reaches at least 60% of the average cell's pre-order rate AND at least 40% of premium pre-orders cite nugget or chewable texture. If premium conversion is under 30% of the average cell, or texture citation is under 15%, reject the premium consumer proposition and move to service-led or OEM options. Anything between is inconclusive and needs a second test.

revisions.reason: SYN-D is a SIMULATED result about a warehouse label printer and packing errors. Even if real, it measures nothing about wearers or home ice buyers, so it changes nothing for T1 or T2. T1 stays as it was, resting on the company's own launch claim, which is still unverified demand evidence. The simulated result is not cited.

Supposing SYN-D were real, it would still measure only packing errors in a warehouse, not consumer ice purchase, pricing or attach revenue. It bears on neither T2's claim about low consumer margins nor its predictions, so T2 is unchanged. The simulated result is not cited.

Supposing the SIMULATED result SYN-D were real: it is a warehouse label-printer test that reduced packing errors, and it measured nothing about wearers or buyers. It bears most weakly on T1, where it would mean nothing about nugget-ice demand, price or attach revenue. T1 stays as it was. This is a what-if only and is not evidence for finish.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer product now. Keep the commercial focus as the default. Before any redesign, run the proposed low-cost pre-order test (X1) of a premium nugget-texture compact home ice maker. Proceed only if it clears the decision rule; otherwise pursue service-led or OEM options.
final.target_customer: Households that already prefer nugget or chewable ice and would buy a dedicated compact machine. This group is a hypothesis; I have no sizing data.
final.value_proposition: A compact home machine that makes nugget-texture ice, sold at a premium with filter or service revenue. Unproven: no price, volume or attach-rate evidence found.
final.next_action: Build a refundable pre-order page with two price cells in one market and run test X1 for about 8 weeks within the proposed EUR 18,500 budget, measuring conversion, texture citation and cost per pre-order against the stated thresholds.
final.uncertainty: No sales, unit or margin data found for Hoshizaki consumer lines. The 2011 Scotsman releases describe a US home nugget-ice machine, but the Alliance excerpt does not list Scotsman, so I cannot confirm Hoshizaki already sells to individuals here. The 'for the first time' claim is unverified seller assertion. No independent consumer demand or pricing data. Budget and thresholds are my proposals; no test has been run; SYN-D was simulated and not used.
would_change_if: X1 premium conversion is below 30% of the average cell, or texture citation below 15%: reject the consumer proposition and move to service-led or OEM.
Sources show Hoshizaki already sells nugget-ice consumer units with strong attach or repeat revenue: T1 gains support.
Independent data show home nugget-ice buyers are few or buy only on price: T2 gains support.

result.brief: Hoshizaki Corporation makes commercial ice machines, refrigerators, dishwashers and dispensers. It is a listed Japanese company that sells through its own direct sales and service network in Japan and through subsidiaries abroad. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. arguments.objective: Decide whether Hoshizaki should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home ice, home beverage or kitchen appliances for individual buyers), or stay commercial-only. Identify the evidence that would justify the investment, and find out how far Hoshizaki already reaches individual buyers before assuming it does not.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Financial and contractual detail may not be public; note what could not be found
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget is 8 searches (7 left), so evidence must be targeted
Must not assume Hoshizaki's current consumer reach; verify it first
alternatives: A. No expansion: remain a commercial ice machine, refrigeration and dispenser maker sold through direct sales and service networks
B. Product redesign: adapt an existing commercial line (for example a compact ice maker) for home or small-office use, sold through existing channels
C. Different route to buyers: sell a consumer-facing range through retail, online or appliance-brand partnerships, leaving Hoshizaki's brand or service in the background
D. Different customer group: serve a specific segment such as small cafés, home-based food businesses, or premium home bar owners rather than mass consumers
E. Service-led proposition: sell maintenance, filter or subscription services to existing installed-base owners, without new hardware for consumers
F. Licensing or OEM supply: supply core compressor or ice-making modules to consumer appliance brands and capture value without owning the consumer relationship
G. Ecosystem or software extension: connected monitoring and replenishment for existing commercial customers, which may open a consumer adjacency later

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition now. Keep the professional-only focus and test a light-duty compact line for small commercial operators through existing distributor and direct channels, using the proposed segment-split probe (X1) before any product investment. Treat the household retail idea as unproven.

frame.objective: Decide whether Tennant Company should invest in a differentiated consumer (individual-buyer) proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional floor-cleaning machines, and identify what evidence would justify that investment rather than assume a consumer market exists.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or intentions known
Company financial and contractual detail may be non-public; must say what could not be found
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining); each search and challenge uses one
Only observed facts may come from read sources; proposed numbers must be labelled as proposed or estimated
Must establish first what Tennant already sells to individual buyers, not assume it
alternatives: No expansion: keep professional-only focus and existing channels
Channel change: sell existing professional machines to individual or small-business buyers via retail or online channels
Product redesign: a smaller, lower-cost or simplified machine for a household or small-space use case
Different customer group: target small commercial operators such as cleaning contractors or small shops with a light-duty line
Partnership or licensing: enter the consumer segment through a brand partner or distributor that already reaches homes, retaining manufacturing
Adjacent consumer use case (for example pet hair, garage or outdoor cleaning) or acquisition of an existing consumer floor-care brand for retail access

T1.claim: Households buy wet-and-dry floor machines to save time and effort on hard floors. A compact, professional-grade scrubber sold through consumer retail could take share from mop-and-bucket and consumer wet-dry machines, so a manufacturer with proven cleaning performance could charge a premium.
T1.who_benefits: Household buyers who want a hard-floor clean with less effort; a manufacturer able to supply a durable, high-performance compact machine.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers already buy wet-dry machines that wash and collect dirty water in one pass (per the Tineco article), so the job is established. A brand with professional-grade performance credentials could shift purchases toward its product on performance and durability.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant sells a branded consumer SKU at a premium price through retail partners, with the same engineering base as its professional range, and keeps the margin rather than paying a brand licence.
assumptions: Consumers value professional-grade durability enough to pay a premium over existing consumer brands
Tennant can access consumer retail shelf space at acceptable margins
A smaller, cheaper version of existing engineering is feasible without a large redesign
Consumer purchase is driven by performance rather than brand or price alone
predictions: In a retail pilot, a Tennant-badged compact machine sells at a price premium to comparable consumer wet-dry machines
Repeat purchase or review ratings are higher than for mid-tier consumer competitors
Retailers agree to shelf space only if the margin is comparable to existing consumer floorcare categories
T1.first_claim: Households buy wet-and-dry floor machines to save time and effort on hard floors. A compact, professional-grade scrubber sold through consumer retail could take share from mop-and-bucket and consumer wet-dry machines, so a manufacturer with proven cleaning performance could charge a premium.

T2.claim: Demand for a compact floor machine comes mainly from small commercial operators such as contractors, small shops and offices, not households. Tennant's value would come from a light-duty professional line sold through its existing distributor and direct channels, not from a consumer brand.
T2.who_benefits: Small commercial operators who need a small-footprint machine for limited floor area and cannot justify a full-size scrubber; Tennant's existing distributor network.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The CS5 Micro-Scrubber was launched for smaller-footprint areas and the claim is that it lets them drop the mop and get a higher level of clean. Operators buy on cleaning quality and labour time, which a professional brand already serves.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant sells a light-duty SKU through its existing professional channels at professional prices, using the service and warranty network it already has, so it captures the margin without building consumer retail.
assumptions: Small commercial operators form a distinct segment with demand for compact machines
Existing distributors will carry a light-duty line without channel conflict
Buyers value service and warranty enough to pay professional prices over consumer alternatives
The consumer use case is not needed to reach this segment
predictions: Distributor orders for a compact line come mainly from small contractors and small retail or office sites, not from home addresses
Compact-line buyers ask for service coverage and warranty terms when choosing between brands
Conversion from mop-and-bucket is highest among small commercial sites with existing cleaning contracts

Tennant's value would come from a light-duty professional line sold through its existing distributor and direct channels, not from a consumer brand.

assessments.quote: a floorcare segment that has grown as consumers seek machines that wash hard floors while collecting dirty water and debris in the same process
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that consumers would pay a premium for a professional-grade Tennant machine over Tineco or others, that retailers would give shelf space, or the size of the premium segment. The 24 million users and 10,000 retail locations are reported by Tineco itself, so they are a company figure, not an independent count.

assessments.quote: The CS5 Micro-Scrubber enables smaller-footprint areas to drop the mop and get a higher level of clean.
assessments.does_not_show: This is Tennant's own launch claim from 2021. It shows that a compact professional product exists for smaller areas. It does not show how many small commercial operators buy it, what they pay, or whether they buy through distributors. It is a product claim, not proof of operator demand.

assessments.quote: The cleaning market as a whole has seen a downward trend recently, primarily due to purchasing restraint among commercial customers
assessments.does_not_show: It is one competitor's press release for 2025, and it does not break out small-operator demand or compact machines. It shows that commercial cleaning purchasing was weak, which lowers the base for a light-duty professional line, but it does not show that small operators stopped buying compact machines or that consumer buyers replaced them.

X1.name: Segment-split demand probe for a compact scrubber
X1.method: Run a two-arm paid-search and landing-page test in one region. Arm A targets households searching for hard-floor wet-and-dry cleaning. Arm B targets small commercial operators (contractors, small shops, offices) and asks for a distributor-quote request. Both arms show the same compact-machine concept and a reserved-price or quote form, with no real product shipped. Test the price point on a split basis (proposed range) to see willingness to pay.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm over 6 weeks, from paid search at a proposed budget of roughly 4,000 euros per arm, plus 15 structured interviews with small commercial operators and 10 with households (estimated).
X1.measure: Qualified reservations or quote requests per 100 visitors by segment; share of quote requests that name a distributor or existing cleaning contract; stated price accepted at each price point; share of households that accept a premium over a known consumer wet-dry price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Household arm converts at least as well as the commercial arm, and households accept a premium over consumer wet-dry prices at the tested price point.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial arm produces most quote requests, many naming an existing distributor or cleaning contract; household arm converts poorly and rejects the premium.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the commercial arm yields at least 2 times the qualified quote requests per 100 visitors of the household arm, and at least 30% of commercial quote requests name a distributor or existing contract, favour T2 and scope a light-duty professional line. If the household arm reaches at least 60% of the commercial conversion and at least 25% accept the premium price, favour T1 and scope a retail pilot. If neither threshold is met, decline further spend and keep both theories open with no investment.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep the professional focus, and test a light-duty compact line for small commercial operators through existing distributor and direct channels before any product investment. Run the proposed segment-split probe (X1) first; its figures are my proposals and it has not been run.
final.target_customer: Small commercial operators (contractors, small shops, offices) with small floor areas. Households are an unproven second segment.
final.value_proposition: A compact, professional-grade scrubber that replaces mop-and-bucket on small areas and gives a higher level of clean, backed by the existing professional service and warranty network. The claim rests on Tennant's own 2021 product statement, not on measured buyer demand.

arguments.name: Segment-split demand probe for a compact scrubber
arguments.method: Run a two-arm paid-search and landing-page test in one region. Arm A targets households searching for hard-floor wet-and-dry cleaning. Arm B targets small commercial operators (contractors, small shops, offices) and asks for a distributor-quote request. Both arms show the same compact-machine concept and a reserved-price or quote form, with no real product shipped. Test the price point on a split basis (proposed range) to see willingness to pay.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm over 6 weeks, from paid search at a proposed budget of roughly 4,000 euros per arm, plus 15 structured interviews with small commercial operators and 10 with households (estimated).
arguments.measure: Qualified reservations or quote requests per 100 visitors by segment; share of quote requests that name a distributor or existing cleaning contract; stated price accepted at each price point; share of households that accept a premium over a known consumer wet-dry price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Household arm converts at least as well as the commercial arm, and households accept a premium over consumer wet-dry prices at the tested price point.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial arm produces most quote requests, many naming an existing distributor or cleaning contract; household arm converts poorly and rejects the premium.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the commercial arm yields at least 2 times the qualified quote requests per 100 visitors of the household arm, and at least 30% of commercial quote requests name a distributor or existing contract, favour T2 and scope a light-duty professional line. If the household arm reaches at least 60% of the commercial conversion and at least 25% accept the premium price, favour T1 and scope a retail pilot. If neither threshold is met, decline further spend and keep both theories open with no investment.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition now. Keep the professional business as the default (Alternative A, with E as a later option). The evidence I could read does not show that individual buyers would pay a premium for a Tennant-made unit through retail (T1) or a recurring service fee (T2). If the company wants to learn more cheaply, run the priced pre-order test X1 in one use case and one market, with the service-led arm as the main test of T2. This is an analyst proposal, not a company plan.

frame.objective: Decide whether Tennant should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case beyond its professional floor-cleaning machines, and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The aim is the highest-value growth option at acceptable risk, not consumer retail for its own sake.
constraints: Outside analyst, public sources only, no company contact or internal data
Search budget of 8, with 7 remaining, and 1 challenge kept for theory testing
Test budget of 20000 EUR and 12 weeks are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Distributor terms, direct-channel economics and segment margins may not be public and must be flagged as unknown
Professional brand, service network and dealer relationships could be diluted or strengthened by a consumer move
Do not assume whether the company already sells to individual buyers; verify first
alternatives: A: No expansion. Keep focus on commercial floor-care machines, direct and distributor sales, and service.
B: Product redesign of existing commercial machines into a smaller, lower-cost unit sold to small commercial buyers and prosumers, without a consumer-brand channel.

C: Different route to buyers: online or home-improvement retail, rental or subscription for individual owners of large hard-floor spaces, or a consumer-branded line for one use case such as garages, workshops or outdoor hard surfaces.

D: Partner or license: a consumer brand or retailer markets a Tennant-engineered product while Tennant keeps manufacturing and service, or acquires an existing consumer floor-care maker for channel and brand.
E: Serve existing professional buyers better through rental, fleet-as-a-service or data services, with no consumer offer.

T1.claim: Individual owners of hard floors will buy a dedicated wet-dry floor washer at a premium if it is sold through mass retail as a home appliance, so a Tennant-engineered compact unit could earn consumer margins that its professional channel cannot.
T1.who_benefits: Individual homeowners with hard-floor spaces, and a manufacturer or brand that reaches them through retail.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumer wet-dry cleaners are already a retail category that people buy for convenience, as shown by Tineco's reported global reach through more than 10,000 retail locations. Buyers are drawn to washing and drying in one pass rather than to commercial-grade capability.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant designs and manufactures a compact unit sold under a consumer brand or licensed to a retailer-facing brand, capturing a per-unit margin plus any licence royalty, without building a consumer sales force.
assumptions: The consumer wet-dry category is large and growing enough to matter to a manufacturer of Tennant's scale
Tennant can build a low-cost consumer unit without diluting its professional brand or service model
Retail buyers accept a non-consumer-native brand and a licensing arrangement
Consumer willingness to pay exceeds the cost of a smaller, lower-spec machine
predictions: Consumer wet-dry sales keep growing faster than commercial floor-machine sales over the next three years
A retailer will take a Tennant-engineered product on a licence at a price that clears a target margin
Pilot buyers in a single retail category show repeat purchase and lower returns than a benchmark consumer brand
T1.first_claim: Individual owners of hard floors will buy a dedicated wet-dry floor washer at a premium if it is sold through mass retail as a home appliance, so a Tennant-engineered compact unit could earn consumer margins that its professional channel cannot.

T2.claim: Individual buyers choose a floor machine partly on whether a repair network stands behind it. Tennant's field service network, which it describes as the most extensive in the industry, is the asset a consumer move would monetise, through service and maintenance income rather than unit margin.
T2.who_benefits: Owners of large hard-floor spaces such as garages, workshops and large homes who want a machine that keeps working, and Tennant through recurring service and rental revenue.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers of a machine that costs more than a basic consumer appliance weigh downtime and repair risk. A visible service promise reduces that risk, so they pay for it, as commercial buyers already do with Tennant.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tennant sells or rents a machine and captures recurring value from service contracts, parts and maintenance, or a subscription, using its existing field service network in the markets it covers.
assumptions: Individual owners value after-sales service enough to pay a recurring fee
Tennant's service network can extend to individual customers at low marginal cost
Service revenue, not unit sales, is the main source of return on a consumer offer

predictions: Individual buyers in a pilot market ask for service terms before price when comparing machines

assessments.quote: a floorcare segment that has grown as consumers seek machines that wash hard floors while collecting dirty water and debris in the same process
assessments.does_not_show: It is a trade-press report about a competitor's category, not Tennant's. It gives no consumer segment size, no margin, no price point, and no sign that a commercial maker could sell a compact unit profitably through retail. The 24 million users and 10,000 retail locations are Tineco's own claims, not verified figures.

assessments.quote: Tennant's global field service network is the most extensive in the industry.
assessments.does_not_show: It is the company's own claim, with no date and no comparison data. It says nothing about whether individual owners value service, will pay a recurring fee, or whether the network reaches home-owner addresses at low marginal cost.

assessments.quote: More than 90% of sales are to professionals while the remaining part of the business aimed at consumers covers floorcare equipment, vacuum cleaners, and high-pressure washers.
assessments.does_not_show: This is one peer's self-reported mix, not Tennant's. It gives no consumer margin, no growth rate for the consumer part, and no reason the consumer share is small: it could reflect weak demand, channel cost, or a deliberate choice to focus. It weakens the claim that consumers are a large prize for a professional maker, but does not show consumers would not buy a Tennant unit.

assessments.quote: The Company reaches these customers through the industry's largest direct sales and service organization and through a strong and well-supported network of authorized distributors worldwide.
assessments.does_not_show: It describes the service network as serving contract cleaners and businesses. It does not say the network serves or is priced for individual owners, nor does it show that individuals would pay a recurring fee. It is neutral on T2 but shows that T2 would require extending a commercial service model into a new customer group, which is untested.

X1.name: Priced pre-order with service versus product-only, one use case, one market
X1.method: Run a landing-page pre-order for a compact wet-dry hard-floor unit aimed at garage and workshop owners in one country. Randomly show three arms: product only at a retail-style price; the same product with a 3-year service plan at a higher bundled price; and the product with a retail-availability message (find-it-in-store) at the retail price. Drive traffic with paid search and social. Pre-orders are refundable deposits, not sales.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 3,000 unique visitors per arm, roughly 9,000 in total, from paid traffic in one country, filtered to people who own a home or workshop with hard floors.
X1.measure: Deposit conversion rate per arm; share of pre-orders that select the service plan; stated willingness to pay; and the email sign-up rate for a retail-availability alert.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Retail-availability arm converts at least as well as the service arm, and the product-only arm at retail price converts well enough to clear a target margin; service plan adds little.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Service-plan arm converts higher and attracts a meaningful share of the service selection, while the retail-availability message adds little.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the service arm's blended revenue per visitor (deposit plus service uptake) exceeds the product-only arm by at least 25 percent, and service selection exceeds 20 percent of pre-orders, favour T2 and scope a service-led pilot. If the retail arm's conversion is within 10 percent of the service arm and product-only clears a proposed 35 percent gross margin at that price, favour T1 and scope a licensing talk. If neither, reject both consumer options and keep Alternative A or E.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition now. Keep the professional business as the default (Alternative A), with a partner or licence route (E) as a later option if a test shows demand. If the company wants to learn more, run the priced pre-order test X1 in one use case and one market, with the service-led arm as the main test of T2. This is an analyst proposal, not a company plan.
final.target_customer: Not yet chosen. A candidate is individual owners of large hard-floor spaces such as garages and workshops, but no individual segment is shown to pay for a Tennant-made product.
final.value_proposition: Untested. A service-backed compact machine (T2) is the more distinctive hypothesis, because the only verified company asset is its service network, but it has not been shown to matter to individual buyers.
final.next_action: Decide whether to fund the proposed 14,000 EUR, 8-week pre-order test X1 (analyst estimate). First, check with the company, which I cannot do from public sources, whether it already sells consumer or prosumer product and what its service margins are.
final.uncertainty: High. No segment margins, distributor terms, channel economics or consumer sales data were public. The 10-Q reports one nonresidential segment. The wet-dry market evidence is trade press on a competitor (Tineco), with self-reported figures. The Nilfisk mix (under 10% consumer) is one peer's claim. T2 rests on one company assertion. My challenge returned no direct contradiction, which means little.
would_change_if: X1 shows the service arm beating product-only by at least 25 percent in revenue per visitor, with service uptake above 20 percent: moves T2 up.
Evidence Tennant already has a profitable consumer or prosumer channel: changes the starting point.
A retailer or licensee paying upfront or royalties for a Tennant-engineered product: supports T1 and licensing (E).
Evidence individuals do not value service, or the network is priced only for commercial contracts: rejects T2.
Data showing consumer sales are small, low-margin or conflict with distributors: strengthens no expansion (A).

X1.name: Consumer concept test: premium wash-and-dry machine with service-message split
X1.method: Online concept test with a mock product page for a compact, detergent-free wash-and-dry hard-floor machine, shown at two price points and two service messages (a local national repair network versus standard manufacturer warranty). Visitors can join a waitlist with a refundable deposit. No product is built and no sale is made. Each arm is a randomised split of paid traffic.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 4,000 visitors from paid online ads targeting UK, German and US households with hard floors, split across four arms of roughly 1,000 each. Plus a 300-person survey panel for willingness-to-pay questions and attitude to repair access.
X1.measure: Waitlist conversion rate by arm, deposit conversion, and stated willingness to pay. Also the share of respondents who rate local repair access as important, from the survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Waitlist conversion is high and similar across service messages, and stated willingness to pay is at least 20 percent above a standard wet-dry machine at the same price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Conversion falls when the service message is weak, the premium is not accepted, and respondents rank repair access as a top purchase factor, so the service message changes intent materially.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the best arm converts at 3 percent or more to a deposit, and the premium arm's conversion is within 30 percent of the standard-price arm, continue to a second stage that includes a retailer conversation. If conversion is under 1 percent in every arm, or the local-service message raises intent by more than 50 percent relative to the standard warranty message, treat T2 as supported and do not proceed to a consumer SKU. Thresholds are proposed, not evidence.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-D is about a warehouse label printer and measured nothing about buyers, so it does not bear on T2. T2 stays on the real sources: the company's own claim of a wide service network and its nonresidential focus. Neither shows that households would value that network. T2 is kept as the more cautious hypothesis, and the concept test remains the way to check it.

SYN-D is a simulated warehouse label-printer result. Even if it were real, it measured nothing about households, prices or detergent-free machines, so it does not bear on T1. T1 stays uncertain and is tested by the proposed concept split, not by this result. T1 is kept as a live hypothesis because the real Tineco market observation shows consumer interest in wash-and-collect floor machines.

Suppose SYN-D were real. It would be a warehouse label-printer result about packing errors, and it measured nothing about buyers. It would bear on T2 only indirectly, as an example of a process gain that says nothing about households. It is SIMULATED, so I do not count it as evidence and do not use it to support or weaken any theory. T2 stays kept on the real sources only: the company's service-network claim and its nonresidential focus.

final.recommendation: Do not build or launch a consumer product now. Keep the professional and distributor focus. Spend no more than the proposed 15,000 EUR concept test (estimated, not run), and treat any consumer product decision as conditional on its result. Public sources show Tennant's business is nonresidential, and they show no household product or consumer revenue line.
final.target_customer: None for now. If a test is run later, the target is hard-floor households in the UK, Germany and the US. This is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
final.value_proposition: No value proposition is supported yet. The untested idea is a compact, detergent-free wash-and-dry machine. The main risk is that households may not value Tennant's professional service network, which is the asset the public evidence points to.
final.next_action: Run the proposed concept test (X1), a six-week online split test of premium price and service message. Continue only if the best arm reaches 3 percent or more deposit conversion, with the premium arm within 30 percent of the standard arm. If Tennant is approached, ask what its 'direct to consumer' sales line means and whether it has household sales data.
final.uncertainty: The evidence is thin. The public sources are mostly company claims: the service network, the nonresidential focus, and the 'direct to consumer' sales figures, which the excerpt does not define. Tineco's user numbers are company claims reported by a trade outlet. I found no public data on Tennant consumer margins, repair costs, distributor agreements or contract terms. The concept test is proposed and has not been run, so both theories are untested.
would_change_if: The concept test shows deposit conversion above the threshold at a premium price, with the service message making little difference, which would support T1 over T2

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer proposition yet. Keep Hoshizaki's commercial focus. Run the X1 pre-order test only as a narrow, paid step, and treat the component (OEM ice module) route as the lower-risk option to study alongside it. Standalone consumer development is unsupported until the test passes its threshold.

frame.objective: Decide whether Hoshizaki should build a differentiated consumer-facing proposition for a specific use case (for example home ice or home kitchen equipment) beyond its commercial foodservice line, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. Judge by expected return on a limited test, not by brand ambition.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Company's consumer reach is unknown and must be established from sources before any theory is built
Financial and contractual detail (distributor terms, channel margins, internal consumer sales) may not be public and must be flagged as unknown
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Searches limited to 8 total; 7 remain after the brief
alternatives: No expansion: keep the commercial focus on foodservice, dealers and service networks and do not enter consumer use cases
Product redesign: adapt an existing commercial ice machine or dispenser into a smaller, lower-cost unit for a home or small-office use case, sold through existing channels
Different route to buyers: sell a consumer-facing product through online retail, appliance retailers or partners, while keeping the commercial service model separate
Different customer group: target small cafés, home-office coffee and bar users or premium home-kitchen buyers who buy like professionals, rather than mass consumers
Licensing or partnership: license the compressor, ice-making or refrigeration technology to an existing consumer appliance brand rather than selling under the Hoshizaki name
Test a narrow pilot in one market before deciding, using the 20000 EUR budget to measure buyer demand and channel response

T1.claim: Home ice-maker buyers are enthusiasts who pay a premium for better-quality ice (clear, nugget or commercial-grade), so a Hoshizaki-engineered home unit sold direct or online to these enthusiasts could earn price premiums over mass-market fridge ice makers.
T1.who_benefits: Enthusiast home buyers who want better ice; Hoshizaki, which would capture a price premium on its ice-making engineering.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Ice quality is a visible, hobby-like attribute. Once buyers see the difference between cloudy cube ice and clear or nugget ice, they value a dedicated machine and pay more for it, as they do for specialist coffee or cocktail equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki sells a branded, higher-priced countertop or under-counter unit through online and specialist retail, keeping margin by not depending on a fridge maker's pricing.
assumptions: A meaningful share of home buyers care about ice quality enough to pay a premium
Hoshizaki can build a home unit at a cost that leaves margin at that premium price
Buyers will purchase a separate appliance rather than rely on the fridge's built-in ice maker
Retail or online channels can reach these buyers without Hoshizaki's foodservice dealer network
predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium ice unit rises among buyers who have seen clear or nugget ice
Conversion from a landing page or pre-order test is higher for an ice-quality message than for a generic 'home ice maker' message
Premium buyers cite ice taste or clarity, not convenience, as the reason for purchase
T1.first_claim: Home ice-maker buyers are enthusiasts who pay a premium for better-quality ice (clear, nugget or commercial-grade), so a Hoshizaki-engineered home unit sold direct or online to these enthusiasts could earn price premiums over mass-market fridge ice makers.

T2.claim: Home ice-maker demand is a built-in feature of the refrigerator, so buyers choose the fridge brand and the ice module is a component. Hoshizaki's value would come from supplying the ice-making module to appliance makers, not from a Hoshizaki-branded product sold to consumers.
T2.who_benefits: Household appliance makers who want an ice feature without developing it; Hoshizaki, which would earn component revenue from its ice technology without consumer marketing or retail costs.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers buy a refrigerator as one purchase, and an automatic ice maker is one of the features they compare. They do not shop for a separate ice machine, so the ice function is valued only as part of the fridge.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Hoshizaki licenses or supplies ice modules to refrigerator manufacturers on a per-unit or contract basis, leaving brand, retail and consumer service to the partner.
assumptions: Consumers treat automatic ice makers as a fridge feature rather than a reason to buy a separate appliance
Fridge makers want to buy ice modules rather than develop them, and Hoshizaki can supply them at a competitive cost
Consumer-facing margin and service costs would make a direct product unattractive for Hoshizaki
predictions: Consumer surveys show ice-maker preference influences fridge choice but rarely drives a separate ice-machine purchase
Fridge makers in target markets already source ice modules from specialist suppliers, creating an OEM route

T1.claim: Homeowners and small-building owners will pay a premium for room-level comfort control that a packaged, contractor-installed retrofit kit delivers, and a component maker that owns the control hardware and the kit design can capture that premium.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and small-building owners who want uneven rooms fixed; HVAC contractors who sell a finished upgrade; Belimo if it captures margin on a kit it designs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners do not buy actuators or dampers; they buy comfort. A packaged, named product with a clear outcome (e.g. one room stops overheating) reframes the purchase as a home improvement, so the buyer accepts a higher price than the parts would cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo designs the kit around its existing actuator and sensor platform and sells it through contractors and distributors, earning a price above the component value, with a repeat stream from service or sensors.
assumptions: Homeowners perceive room-to-room temperature imbalance as a real problem worth paying to fix
Contractors will stock and recommend a Belimo-branded kit
Existing actuators can be packaged without a costly redesign or new certifications
Belimo's 2015 residential launch (select actuators, round dampers, pressure bypass controls) shows the product line can reach residential use
predictions: Contractors who are offered the kit at a retail-style margin will place it on a meaningful share of retrofit quotes
Homeowners shown a comfort-outcome price will convert at a rate that covers the kit's cost of sale
Sales of the 2015 residential range, if their volumes can be found, will be small relative to commercial sales
T1.first_claim: Homeowners and small-building owners will pay a premium for room-level comfort control that a packaged, contractor-installed retrofit kit delivers, and a component maker that owns the control hardware and the kit design can capture that premium.

T2.claim: Homeowners do not choose HVAC components, and installing contractors and OEMs control the purchase decision, so a consumer-facing Belimo brand would mostly reach buyers through the same B2B channels; the value Belimo can capture from consumers is therefore limited to component supply and licensing to brands that own the consumer relationship.
T2.who_benefits: OEMs and HVAC contractors, who keep the customer relationship and brand; Belimo if it supplies components and earns volume without bearing consumer marketing, service or warranty costs.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners rely on the installer's recommendation and on the equipment brand's warranty, so they seldom pick a damper or actuator maker. Contractors pick components for reliability and install speed, not brand pull, so Belimo's leverage stays with specification by OEMs and contractors.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo keeps its position as a specified component supplier, earning volume and margin from OEM and integrator relationships and possibly from licensing its control firmware or sensors to consumer smart-home brands, avoiding the cost of building a consumer brand.
assumptions: Consumer buying of HVAC hardware is driven by installer and brand recommendation, not component brand
Belimo's existing channel to OEMs and contractors is strong and extensible
Consumer smart-home brands would pay for certified actuator or sensor components
predictions: Installers asked which damper or actuator brand they would specify will name the OEM or equipment brand first, not the component maker
Consumer smart-home brands that use third-party actuators or sensors will do so under their own brand, with no visible component-maker logo
A direct-to-consumer test of a Belimo-branded product will generate far fewer orders per marketing euro than the same offer routed through a contractor
