assessments.does_not_show: Whether homeowners want room-level comfort control, whether any buyer paid a premium, whether contractors stocked or recommended these products, or what volumes were sold. It is a 2015 launch announcement of components for residential use, not a packaged consumer kit, and it is not evidence of demand.

assessments.quote: The focus of its core business is on damper actuators, control valves, sensors and meters.
assessments.does_not_show: How consumers or homeowners choose HVAC components, whether installers or OEMs control specification, whether Belimo's channel could carry a consumer brand, or any revenue split by customer type. It shows the company describes its core as field devices, not that contractor gatekeeping holds.

assessments.quote: more than two-thirds of those households control temperatures without actually programming the thermostat
assessments.does_not_show: Whether homeowners would pay for a packaged room-comfort kit, whether contractor-installed retrofits sell, or what the premium would be. It is a 2017 US statistic about thermostat programming, which weakens T1's assumption that homeowners engage with control features, but does not rule out paying for a comfort outcome.

X1.name: Contractor-led room-comfort kit pre-order test
X1.method: Recruit about 15 HVAC contractors in one metro area under a non-binding pilot agreement. Contractors offer a named room-comfort retrofit kit (using existing Belimo actuator and sensor parts, as a mock-up or priced prototype) to homeowners with a known room-temperature complaint. Run a parallel direct-to-homeowner landing page that routes buyers to those contractors. Compare reservation rates for a comfort-outcome price against a parts-price offer and against an offer shown with the contractor's brand only, to see whether the Belimo name adds any pull.
X1.sample: Proposed: 15 contractors; about 400 homeowner landing-page visitors who submit a room-comfort problem form; about 60 homeowners receiving a quote. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Share of quoted homeowners who place a refundable reservation at the target price; number of contractors who agree to stock the kit; share of contractors who name the equipment brand rather than Belimo when asked which component they would specify.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners who receive a comfort-outcome quote reserve at a meaningful rate, and contractors stock the kit when offered a retail-style margin.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowner reservations stay low and are no higher with the Belimo name shown; contractors specify by equipment brand and decline to stock a component-brand kit.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a scaled pilot only if at least 3 percent of quoted homeowners reserve at the target price and at least 5 of 15 contractors agree to stock the kit with the Belimo name visible. Otherwise keep the B2B focus (T2) and do not build a consumer brand. Thresholds are proposed analyst values, not company figures.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer brand now. Keep the core B2B focus on HVAC field devices. The public evidence shows Belimo has residential-applicable components (2015 launch) and describes its core as commercial field devices, but it shows no consumer sales, no homeowner demand and no contractor uptake for a packaged kit. Only a cheap, contractor-led test is justified before any consumer investment.
final.target_customer: Current B2B customers (OEMs, HVAC contractors, system integrators) remain the core. A consumer or small-building route is only worth testing through contractors.
final.value_proposition: Unproven. The only candidate is a Belimo-designed room-comfort retrofit kit sold through contractors, which would need to show homeowner reservations and contractor stocking before it is a proposition at all.
final.next_action: Scope a contractor-first pilot (proposed X1, about EUR 18,000 over 10 weeks, est.) with about 15 contractors and a homeowner landing page. Before running it, ask Belimo's management or investor relations for residential sales and channel data, which I could not find in public sources.
final.uncertainty: High. I found no Belimo financial split by customer type, no residential revenue, and no information on the 2015 residential range's volumes or whether it still sells. The Resideo article is about a competitor, undated, and was used only as context. The 2017 EIA statistic on thermostat programming is US-only and dated. The test X1 is a proposal; nothing has been run. Thresholds (3 percent reservation, 5 of 15 contractors) are analyst estimates.

frame.objective: Decide whether Tennant Company should invest in a differentiated consumer (individual-buyer) proposition for a specific use case beyond its professional floor-cleaning machines, and identify what evidence would justify that investment, using public sources only.

alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the professional-only model, direct in 21 countries and distributors in 100+ countries
B. Product redesign: adapt an existing professional machine, for example a compact or battery model, for smaller commercial or home-adjacent use through existing channels
C. Different route to buyers: sell existing or lightly adapted machines to individuals via retail, online or rental channels, with no new product
D. Different customer group: target a specific consumer use case such as home or prosumer floor care, or small self-employed cleaners, with a purpose-built product
E. Partnership or licensing: enter the consumer segment through a consumer appliance brand or retailer, with Tennant supplying technology or manufacturing and keeping the professional brand separate
F. Accessory or service extension: sell consumables, maintenance subscriptions or rental to existing professional customers, which is adjacent rather than consumer-facing

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tennant designs and sells a compact model under its own brand, possibly through retail or online, earning consumer-level margin on a product derived from its professional engineering

Tennant can build a compact product at a cost that leaves a margin at retail prices

X1.name: Compact unit: Tennant-branded vs partner-branded sell-through pilot
X1.method: Proposed: a 12-week paired pilot in a small number of retail or online listings. A compact commercial-grade unit is listed at a price near premium consumer wet-dry machines, once under a Tennant brand and once under a neutral or partner brand, with the same product, price and listing quality. Compare sell-through, price realised, and post-purchase reasons for buying.

position.recommendation: Do not build a consumer brand yet. If Belimo pursues residential demand at all, test it first through its existing installer and contractor channel with a residential zone-control kit, using the 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot as a gate. No evidence I read shows Belimo sells to individual buyers today; its public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels only.

T1.claim: Belimo's value in residential heating control is captured through installers and contractors, not individual buyers. Homeowners and landlords adopt zone control when a qualified installer recommends and fits it, so the installer channel Belimo already serves is the route to demand.
T1.who_benefits: HVAC installers and controls contractors, who earn installation margin and avoid callbacks; then homeowners and landlords who get working zone control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Installers already sell and fit commercial and light-commercial controls. A product that fits their workflow, has training behind it, and reduces commissioning failures gives them a reason to recommend it to residential customers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo sells components through distributors and installer networks, using the technical support and HVAC professional training its annual report describes, rather than building a consumer brand.
assumptions: Installers would bring residential zone-control jobs to Belimo-based products if the product is simple to fit
Residential retrofit jobs run through contractors who already buy from the manufacturer's channel
Installer margin is large enough to change their recommendation
predictions: In a pilot with installers, quote and attachment rates for residential zone control exceed those for direct-to-consumer ads

T2.claim: Homeowners buy heating control directly from the brand when they see the energy saving themselves, as tado and Nest did. A consumer-branded product sold online can therefore capture value that installer channels do not reach.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters who want lower heating bills and control from an app, and the brand that owns the customer relationship and the subscription or repeat revenue.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Heating bills are visible and frequent, so a clear saving claim and an app make the purchase feel like a comfort and cost decision rather than a building-services job.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo would sell a retail or online product and keep the margin that installers and distributors take in the B2B channel.
assumptions: Homeowners can install or accept a self-fit product without a contractor

X1.name: Installer-referral versus direct-online pilot for residential zone control
X1.method: Two-arm pilot in one metro area with one residential zone-control kit (existing hardware, no new product). Arm A: sell through 10 to 15 installers who fit the kit and quote homeowners and landlords. Arm B: run online paid search and social ads with a self-fit or installer-finder CTA, sending buyers to the same kit. Track quotes, sales and callbacks for 8 weeks after a 2-week setup.
X1.sample: Proposed: 10 to 15 installers and about 1,500 ad-driven visitors split over 8 weeks. Budget and sample sizes are estimates for this exercise.
X1.measure: Quote-to-sale conversion per arm; cost per acquired customer per arm; installer-reported callbacks per 10 installs; share of ad buyers who request an installer.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A converts quotes to sales at a higher rate than Arm B, with fewer callbacks, and a meaningful share of Arm B buyers asks for an installer, showing demand routes through installers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B cost per acquired customer falls below gross margin per unit, and few Arm B buyers ask for an installer, showing homeowners buy direct.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: favour T2 only if Arm B cost per customer is below 60 percent of unit gross margin and under 20 percent of Arm B buyers request an installer. Favour T1 if Arm A quote-to-sale conversion is at least 1.5 times Arm B and Arm A callbacks are at most half of the national baseline. Otherwise keep both theories open.

final.recommendation: Do not start a consumer brand now. Belimo's public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels, and I found no evidence that it sells to individual buyers today. If management wants residential demand, test it first through the installer channel with a residential zone-control kit, gated by a 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot. The pilot is a proposal and has not been run.
final.target_customer: Installers and controls contractors serving residential and small-landlord retrofits (provisional, untested). Direct homeowners are a secondary segment to test, not a target yet.
final.value_proposition: A residential-fit zone-control kit that installers can fit and commission with fewer callbacks, backed by the technical support and training Belimo already gives HVAC professionals. Unproven.
final.next_action: Run the proposed two-arm pilot (X1), installer-referral arm versus direct-online arm, with the decision rule as proposed. First confirm how installers in the target market are paid and recruited, and check the company's own residential sales data, which is not public.
final.uncertainty: High. Belimo's own residential sales, channel mix, margins, installer economics and acquisition costs are not public. The Belimo sources are company self-descriptions. Consumer comparisons (tado, Nest, Airthings, Resideo) are other companies' results and do not show Belimo could replicate them. Airthings reported 2025 consumer revenue down 20% while its professional segment grew, which weakens the consumer case. The pilot figures are my estimates.

arguments.name: Installer-referral versus direct-online pilot for residential zone control
arguments.method: Two-arm pilot in one metro area with one residential zone-control kit (existing hardware, no new product). Arm A: sell through 10 to 15 installers who fit the kit and quote homeowners and landlords. Arm B: run online paid search and social ads with a self-fit or installer-finder CTA, sending buyers to the same kit. Track quotes, sales and callbacks for 8 weeks after a 2-week setup.
arguments.sample: Proposed: 10 to 15 installers and about 1,500 ad-driven visitors split over 8 weeks. Budget and sample sizes are estimates for this exercise.
arguments.measure: Quote-to-sale conversion per arm; cost per acquired customer per arm; installer-reported callbacks per 10 installs; share of ad buyers who request an installer.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A converts quotes to sales at a higher rate than Arm B, with fewer callbacks, and a meaningful share of Arm B buyers asks for an installer, showing demand routes through installers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B cost per acquired customer falls below gross margin per unit, and few Arm B buyers ask for an installer, showing homeowners buy direct.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: favour T2 only if Arm B cost per customer is below 60 percent of unit gross margin and under 20 percent of Arm B buyers request an installer. Favour T1 if Arm A quote-to-sale conversion is at least 1.5 times Arm B and Arm A callbacks are at most half of the national baseline. Otherwise keep both theories open.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a consumer brand yet. If Belimo pursues residential demand at all, test it first through its existing installer and contractor channel with a residential zone-control kit, using the 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot as a gate. No evidence I read shows Belimo sells to individual buyers today; its public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels only.

Do not start a consumer brand now. Belimo's public material describes OEM, integrator and HVAC-professional channels. I found no evidence that it sells to individual buyers today. If management wants residential demand, test it first through the installer channel with a residential zone-control kit, gated by a 20000 EUR, 12-week pilot. The test is only a proposal and has not been run.
arguments.target_customer: Installers and controls contractors serving residential and small-landlord retrofits (provisional, untested). Direct homeowners are a secondary segment to test, not a target yet.
arguments.value_proposition: A residential-fit zone-control kit that installers can fit and commission with less callback risk, supported by the technical support and training Belimo already gives HVAC professionals. Unproven.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed two-arm pilot (X1): installer-referral arm versus direct-online arm, with the decision rule as proposed, and first confirm how installers in the target market are paid and recruited. Before spending, check the company's own residential sales data, which is not public.
arguments.uncertainty: High. The key evidence about Belimo's own residential sales, channel mix, margins, installer economics and customer acquisition cost is not public. The only Belimo sources I read are company self-descriptions. The consumer-brand comparisons (tado, Nest, Airthings, Resideo) are other companies' results from news or their own sites, and do not show Belimo could replicate them. Airthings reported consumer revenues down 20% in 2025 while its professional segment grew, which weakens the consumer case. I did not find a dedicated study of homeowner willingness to pay for zone control. The pilot figures are my estimates.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Installers specify a zoning solution when it is pre-engineered, has a single part number and comes with commissioning support. That lowers their risk and time on retrofits, so they recommend it to the homeowner.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo sells a bundled kit (actuators, round dampers, bypass control, commissioning tool) through its existing distributors and contractors, at a price above loose components. Revenue comes from kit sales and repeat actuator demand.

Belimo's existing distributors can reach residential installers without a new channel

T2.claim: Homeowners do not buy zoning or damper hardware under the component maker's name. The brand that the homeowner sees and trusts is the thermostat or system brand, and that brand keeps the value. A component maker's residential line therefore earns little beyond the component sale, because the consumer-facing brand and the installer relationship sit with others.
T2.who_benefits: Thermostat and system brands (for example Resideo or Honeywell) and the installers who recommend them. They control the consumer-facing purchase and the brand trust.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners buy comfort outcomes and trust the brand on the thermostat. An actuator maker that is invisible to the homeowner cannot shift that choice, so installers and system brands keep the decision and the margin.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Value stays with the thermostat or system brand, which sells the consumer proposition. Belimo's residential components sell as low-margin inputs, unless it licenses or supplies the control logic to those brands.

X1.name: Installer kit versus loose components, residential zoning pilot
X1.method: Recruit residential HVAC installers who already buy Belimo actuators through an existing distributor. Randomly offer half a pre-engineered zoning kit (single part number, pre-set bypass control, commissioning guide, phone support) and half the same parts sold loose at the same total price. Track orders, time to commission each zone, and callbacks for 12 weeks. Installers not offered the kit are not contacted.
X1.sample: Proposed: 40 to 60 installers across 2 to 3 regional distributors, each with at least 5 residential retrofit jobs a month. Target about 200 zone jobs in total.
X1.measure: Share of zone jobs bought as the kit versus loose parts. Median commissioning time per zone. Callbacks within 90 days. Also record which thermostat or system brand each job uses, to check whether the system brand decides the choice.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Installers in the kit arm buy the kit for a clear majority of zone jobs, commissioning time falls, and callbacks fall, because the kit lowers their labour and risk.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Kit uptake stays low and is driven by the system or thermostat brand the installer is already using. Commissioning time and callbacks do not differ much between arms, because installers still choose and assemble their own parts.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: continue to a larger residential programme only if at least 40 percent of kit-arm zone jobs use the kit and median commissioning time is at least 20 percent shorter than in the loose arm. If kit uptake is below 15 percent, or if the system brand explains most of the uptake differences, stop the residential consumer line and keep Belimo as a component supplier.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer-branded product now. Keep Belimo's core as a B2B component supplier. If management wants to test residential value, run the capped installer-kit pilot (X1) first, since it is the only route in the evidence that could capture value without a consumer brand. No public evidence found of Belimo residential sales at scale.
final.target_customer: Residential HVAC installers and controls contractors who already buy Belimo actuators, as the pilot target. Homeowners are not a direct target at this stage.
final.value_proposition: A pre-engineered residential zoning kit (single part number, pre-set bypass control, commissioning guide, support) that cuts installer labour and callbacks. This is a hypothesis to test, not a validated proposition.
final.next_action: Run pilot X1 with installers through an existing distributor, after checking the company's own residential sales and channel data, which I could not see. Stop if the decision rule fails: kit uptake below 15 percent, or the system brand explains most of the uptake.
final.uncertainty: Large. The 2015 launch shows residential components were offered, not whether they sold, to whom, or at what margin. Sales, channel, pricing and contract data are not public. I read three relevant sources and one unrelated Tado article. The 2026 annual report describes a commercial focus. The Resideo item is undated vendor copy. Pilot costs and thresholds are my proposals. Belief: T2 likely, T1 uncertain.

T1.claim: Homeowners buy zoning and damper control as a comfort upgrade when a contractor specifies it, so a residential zone kit sold through the existing HVAC contractor channel can earn a price premium.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Comfort complaints and uneven rooms prompt a service call, and the contractor recommends a zone fix that is cheaper than replacing the system
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo sells residential-rated actuators, round dampers and bypass controls to contractors and distributors as a packaged zone kit, keeping its brand inside the contractor's quote
assumptions: Homeowners do not choose the component brand; the installing contractor does
Zoning retrofits are common enough in the target homes to support a product line
Belimo's existing residential-application products (2015) can be packaged without a new product platform
predictions: Sales of residential-rated Belimo parts grow where contractors actively sell zoning
Contractors who stock the kit quote it in a larger share of comfort-complaint jobs
Homeowners ask for zoning by room, not by component brand

T2.why_behaviour_changes: A visible savings figure or an alert about a fault gives the homeowner a reason to act or to pay for a service, and the purchase is made on the outcome rather than on the parts
T2.how_value_is_captured: A subscription or service fee for monitoring and fault alerts, sold direct or through installers, with sensors as the entry hardware
assumptions: Homeowners will pay a recurring fee for energy data they cannot get from their existing thermostat
Belimo's sensing and analytics can be delivered to a home without a large new software platform
The installer, not the homeowner, may still be the gate to the purchase
predictions: Homeowners who see a savings figure are more likely to keep paying a subscription after the first year

X1.name: Contractor-channel zone kit pilot with a parallel savings-subscription price test
X1.method: Two-arm pilot in one metro area. Arm A: recruit about 20 HVAC contractors to offer a residential zone kit (residential-rated actuators, round dampers and bypass controls, using existing Belimo parts or a prototype kit) on comfort-complaint jobs for 8 weeks, tracking how often it is quoted and accepted. Arm B: a landing page offering a monitoring and savings-alert service at a proposed monthly fee, with a pre-order or deposit, shown to homeowners by paid search and contractor referral.
X1.sample: Arm A: about 20 contractors and their comfort-complaint jobs (proposed). Arm B: about 1,000 homeowner visitors to the landing page (proposed), with at least 30 homeowners reaching the pre-order step.
X1.measure: Arm A: share of comfort-complaint quotes that include the zone kit, and accepted-quote rate. Arm B: pre-order conversion rate from landing-page visits, and share of pre-orders that keep paying after month one.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Contractors quote the zone kit on a meaningful share of comfort-complaint jobs and the homeowner accepts it; the homeowner does not ask for a named component brand.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Homeowners pre-order the monitoring service at a steady conversion rate and keep paying after month one, and the zone kit is quoted rarely because the homeowner does not frame the problem as a zoning fix.

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a larger T1 pilot only if at least 15% of comfort-complaint quotes from participating contractors include the zone kit and at least 40% of those quotes are accepted within 8 weeks. Pursue the T2 subscription only if pre-order conversion is at least 3% of landing visits and at least 60% of pre-orders are still paying after month one. If neither threshold is met, do not invest further in a consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The only simulated result, SYN-D, concerns a label printer's packing errors and measured nothing about homeowners, contractors or zone products, so it would not change T1. T1 stays as before: supported only by the 2015 product announcement, with demand and contractor pull still untested.

SYN-D is simulated and concerns label-printer packing errors, not homeowners or monitoring. Even if it were real it would not bear on T2, so T2 stays as before with no evidence for or against it. It is not cited in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build a standalone consumer brand yet. Run a small residential zone-kit pilot through the existing HVAC contractor channel, and treat the homeowner monitoring subscription as a cheap side test only. Stop if neither threshold is met.
final.target_customer: Homeowners with comfort complaints (uneven rooms), reached through HVAC contractors, not direct-to-consumer
final.value_proposition: A residential zone kit that contractors can quote as a comfort fix, using residential-rated Belimo actuators, round dampers and bypass controls
final.next_action: Recruit about 20 contractors in one metro area for an 8-week zone-kit quoting pilot (proposed cost about EUR 18,000 over 12 weeks, an estimate). Proceed to a larger pilot only if at least 15% of comfort-complaint quotes include the kit and at least 40% of those are accepted.
final.uncertainty: Belimo's current residential sales, margins and contracts are not public, so I could not confirm the 2015 residential line still sells. I found no source on homeowner zoning demand. The only consumer-facing source was a Resideo launch, about another company. My challenge search found nothing against T1, but it was thin. T2 has no evidence beyond the company's commercial focus.

T1.claim: Belimo's residential offering is a component extension of its existing zone-control know-how. Residential installers and HVAC retrofit contractors need actuators and dampers for zoning, and Belimo can sell these through its existing distributor and contractor channel without owning a consumer brand.
T1.who_benefits: Residential HVAC installers and retrofit contractors, who need reliable zone components; Belimo, which sells more of the same parts into a new segment.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Installers choose components that are easy to specify, cheap to fit and supported by the supplier. A residential SKU range reduces their search and callbacks, so they switch to or add Belimo parts.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo earns component margin on units sold through its existing contractor and distributor network. It keeps the end-customer relationship with the installer, so it avoids consumer marketing and app costs.

Belimo's existing distribution reaches residential installers
Residential SKUs can share the commercial product platform at acceptable cost

T1.first_claim: Belimo's residential offering is a component extension of its existing zone-control know-how. Residential installers and HVAC retrofit contractors need actuators and dampers for zoning, and Belimo can sell these through its existing distributor and contractor channel without owning a consumer brand.

T2.claim: Consumer smart-thermostat and smart-heating markets are too fragmented for a single consumer brand to scale across Europe, because heating systems differ by country and by home. The value sits with the component supplier that adapts to many system types, which means selling to smart-home brands rather than building a Belimo consumer product.
T2.who_benefits: Smart-home brands such as tado and other thermostat makers, which need valves and actuators that work across varied European heating systems; Belimo, if it supplies them as an OEM component.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A thermostat brand that cannot cover the range of heating systems in its market must either narrow its product or buy compatible hardware. It is more likely to buy a proven component that fits many systems than to build its own actuator and valve line.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo earns component revenue per unit supplied to consumer brands, or licensing income. It avoids consumer brand costs, retail costs and the risk of a failed consumer launch.

X1.method: Two parallel low-cost checks in one European market. Arm A: offer a residential zone kit (existing actuators and dampers in a residential bundle) to a set of residential HVAC installers through an existing distributor, and record orders and reorders. Arm B: approach smart-thermostat brands with a component sample and a one-page spec, and record whether any brand agrees to a paid evaluation.
X1.sample: Proposed: 25 residential installers or contractors in one country, and 8 smart-heating brands or valve OEMs. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Arm A: number of installers placing a first order within 8 weeks, and reorders within 12 weeks. Arm B: number of brands agreeing to a paid evaluation or sample test within 12 weeks.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Several installers place first orders and reorder, because they need zoning parts and the product fits their existing supply relationship. Brand interest in Arm B is low.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Installer orders are sparse and reorders are rare, because installers buy whole systems from established suppliers. Several brands ask for paid evaluations, because they need compatible components across heating types.

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if at least 6 of 25 installers (24%) place a first order and at least 3 reorder within 12 weeks. Favour T2 if fewer than 3 installers order and at least 2 of 8 brands agree to a paid evaluation. If both thresholds are met or neither is, neither theory is supported and the investigation stops with no expansion.

revisions.reason: SYN-D is a simulated warehouse test of a label printer. It is not real and measured nothing about installers, homeowners or zone components, so it changes nothing for T1. T1 stays unchanged on the strength of the 2015 Belimo residential announcement, which is the only real evidence bearing on it.

SYN-D is a simulated warehouse label-printer test. It is not real and measured nothing about heating brands, OEM components or buyers, so it changes nothing for T2. T2 stays unchanged on the strength of the Google statement and the tado report, which are the real evidence bearing on it.

Supposing SYN-D were real, it is a warehouse label-printer test and would bear on packing accuracy, not on residential installers or zone components. So even as a what-if it would change nothing for T1. T1 stays as it is. It is not cited as evidence in the finish.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. Keep the professional and institutional focus as the base case, and run the low-cost discharge-and-institution test before any consumer investment. The evidence I could read does not settle whether individuals buy home CPR training at a scale worth a dedicated product. A consumer kit at about 30 USD existed in 2006, which weakens my earlier view that individuals will not buy at all. But I found no sales data, no evidence that the consumer line is still sold, and the one household-distribution example (NICU kits) was a donation with no take-up or revenue figures. The ILCOR source also says high-risk families often do not take up training, which cuts against T1's uptake assumption.

T1.claim: Individuals rarely buy CPR training for themselves, but households with a specific trigger (a newborn in intensive care, a family member with heart disease) will train at home when the kit arrives at a moment of need, so a targeted home kit sold through hospitals or health programmes can earn revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Families at a high-risk moment (e.g. parents of babies discharged from neonatal intensive care) and the hospitals or health funders who want to give them training.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Fear and a sense of responsibility after a serious health event make the lesson urgent and personal, and a kit given at discharge removes the search, cost and effort of finding training.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal supplies kit hardware or content to hospitals, charities or insurers' foundations on a per-kit or bulk-order basis, rather than selling to each individual consumer.
assumptions: Families accept and use a home kit when it is given at discharge
Hospitals or funders will pay for kits at a price that covers manufacturing and distribution
Kit use leads to repeat or wider household training, not just one-off use
predictions: Uptake of kits given at discharge is high (e.g. above 50 percent of families) when they are free or hospital-prescribed
Uptake falls sharply when the same kit must be bought at retail
Kit distribution is repeated by other hospitals or funders within a few years
T1.first_claim: Individuals rarely buy CPR training for themselves, but households with a specific trigger (a newborn in intensive care, a family member with heart disease) will train at home when the kit arrives at a moment of need, so a targeted home kit sold through hospitals or health programmes can earn revenue.

T2.claim: Individual consumers will not buy CPR training for themselves at a meaningful price, but employers, schools and public programmes buy it because of mandates, liability and training obligations. Value therefore sits in institutional bundles, not in a consumer product.
T2.who_benefits: Employers, schools and community programmes that must show staff or pupils are trained, and the training providers who sell to them.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Compliance requirements, insurance and duty-of-care obligations make training a cost of operating, so the buyer is motivated by obligation rather than personal desire.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Laerdal sells manikins, kits and training programmes to institutions in volume, using existing B2B relationships and certification partnerships, so a consumer line adds little beyond what the institutional channel already captures.

X1.name: Discharge-offer take-up test with price point
X1.method: Partner with one neonatal or cardiac follow-up unit willing to offer a home CPR kit at a stated price (proposed: 25 EUR, with a free option for those who ask) to families at discharge. In parallel, offer the same kit to one employer or school group in the same catchment as an institutional bundle. Record offers, purchases and completion of the training module at 4 weeks. Pricing and sample are proposed, not company figures.
X1.sample: About 150 eligible families at discharge and 2 institutional groups of about 30 people each (proposed; needs partner agreement and ethics or data sign-off)
X1.measure: Share of offered families who buy or take the kit; share who complete the training module within 4 weeks; share of institutional group who buy the bundle

prediction_by_theory.T1: Take-up at discharge is at least 30 percent at the stated price, and at least 70 percent of buyers complete training within 4 weeks, showing that the moment of need drives purchase
prediction_by_theory.T2: Take-up at discharge stays below 10 percent at the stated price, while the institutional group buys at a higher rate, showing that individuals do not pay for training and institutions do

X1.decision_rule: Proceed to a consumer pilot only if discharge take-up is 30 percent or more AND completion is 70 percent or more. If take-up is below 10 percent and institutional purchase exceeds discharge take-up, treat T2 as favoured and do not invest in a consumer line. Anything between is inconclusive and triggers a second, larger test rather than investment.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition now. Keep professional and institutional focus as the base case, and run the proposed discharge-and-institution test (X1) before deciding. The evidence I could read does not show that individuals buy home CPR training at a scale that justifies a dedicated product, nor that the consumer line earns meaningful revenue today.
final.target_customer: Not yet chosen. Candidates are families at a high-risk moment (e.g. parents discharged from neonatal intensive care) and institutional buyers (employers, schools, community programmes). Institutions are better supported on current evidence.
final.value_proposition: A home or family CPR kit offered at discharge or through an institutional bundle. This is a hypothesis, not a tested proposition.
final.next_action: Scope X1 with one partner hospital unit and one institutional group: confirm partner agreement, ethics or data sign-off, kit price and supplier. Check whether Laerdal's CPR Anytime consumer line is still sold and at what price. Run X1 only if scoping confirms sample and cost, and apply the decision rule as written.
final.uncertainty: High. No Laerdal sales, revenue or margin data for consumer kits was found, so profitability and current status are unknown. The NICU kit donation came from the AHA with a foundation's funding; the source does not say Laerdal made the kits. The 2006 consumer product article gives no volumes. The ILCOR source suggests high-risk families often do not take up training, but gives no rates. Contract terms and institutional pricing are non-public. Search budget was limited.
would_change_if: Laerdal sales data or a public filing shows consumer kit revenue is material and growing (favours T1)
X1 shows discharge take-up at or above 30 percent with 70 percent or more completing training (proposed threshold; favours T1 and a consumer pilot)
X1 shows discharge take-up below 10 percent while institutional purchase is higher (confirms T2)
A regulator or insurer mandates home or family CPR training for high-risk groups (strengthens an institutional bundle)
Evidence the 2006 consumer product was discontinued or had small retail sales (strengthens T2)

T1.claim: Lay CPR training sells to individuals mainly at moments of salient risk, such as a new baby leaving intensive care or a family member's cardiac diagnosis. A kit bought or donated at those moments, and sold through hospitals and cardiac services, could earn Laerdal a repeatable, trigger-based revenue stream.
T1.who_benefits: Families at a known risk moment, and the hospital or charity that wants to hand over a kit at discharge; Laerdal if it supplies the kit and content
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A specific, dated threat makes a 20-minute skill feel urgent and worth doing, and the clinical setting gives a trusted reason to take it up. Ordinary, low-salience consumers do not act.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Per-kit sales or supply contracts to hospital and charity programmes at discharge points, with possible repeat purchases for other family members
assumptions: Uptake depends on the discharge or diagnosis moment, not on general awareness
Hospitals or charities, not families, pay for the kits
The kit's content can be delivered without an instructor
predictions: Uptake of kits handed out at discharge is much higher than uptake of the same kit offered by post or online to the general public
Hospital programmes that buy kits repeat orders year on year
Public sales of the same kit without a clinical trigger stay small
T1.first_claim: Lay CPR training sells to individuals mainly at moments of salient risk, such as a new baby leaving intensive care or a family member's cardiac diagnosis. T2.claim: Individuals will not pay for CPR training, so the value sits with institutional funders such as foundations, insurers and employers that pay for distribution. Laerdal's realistic route is to supply the hardware and content to those funders, not to build a direct consumer brand.
T2.who_benefits: Funders such as foundations and insurers that want to be seen funding lifesaving, and the charities that deliver the training; Laerdal as supplier of kits and content
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Funders have a reputational and programme reason to buy at scale, so they buy kits that individuals would not buy for themselves. Individuals take the kit once it is handed to them free or at low cost.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Bulk supply and licensing contracts with funders and programme operators, with Laerdal earning on units and content rather than consumer margins
assumptions: Funders buy at scale when a grant or sponsor is attached

Laerdal can supply kits without taking on consumer marketing costs

Laerdal's involvement is as supplier, with the funder holding the customer relationship

X1.name: Trigger-point versus open-channel kit offer
X1.method: Two-arm field test with a neutral, identical CPR home-practice kit. Arm A: offered at discharge or a clinic visit by a partner hospital for families with a recent high-risk event. Arm B: offered online to the general public at the same price. Arm C: funder-paid kit given free through a charity or employer scheme. Uptake and completed practice measured at 4 and 8 weeks.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 300 families per arm, recruited through 2 partner hospitals or cardiac clinics and one charity, with consent. Cost and partner access are estimates to be confirmed.
X1.measure: Proportion who take up the kit (paid or accepted), proportion who complete the practice session at 8 weeks, and the price paid per unit where relevant

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A uptake is clearly higher than Arm B at the same price, and Arm B stays low
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm C (funder-paid) has the highest uptake, and Arm B and Arm A both show low willingness to pay, so price sales do not reach the trigger-based level

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if Arm A uptake is at least 2 times Arm B uptake and Arm A paid uptake is at least 15 per cent (proposed threshold). Favour T2 if Arm C uptake is at least 2 times Arm A, and Arm A paid uptake is below 5 per cent. If neither holds, treat both as weak and stop.

Even if SYN-D were real, a warehouse label-printer result says nothing about who buys or distributes CPR kits, so it would not move T2. T2 is unchanged and still rests on the funder-paid donation report, which shows funder-paid distribution but not its share of volume.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a broad consumer proposition yet. Laerdal already sells a home CPR kit (CPR Anytime) direct, but the sources I could read show no sales volumes, prices or margins, so consumer scale and profit are unproven. The most promising narrow case is a trigger-point offer: a kit handed over at a known risk moment, such as discharge of a high-risk infant, delivered through a clinical or charity partner. Test it against an open online offer and a funder-paid route before investing.
final.target_customer: Families at a recent high-risk point, such as parents discharged from neonatal intensive care, with hospitals or charities as buyers or distributors. Not the general public, pending the test.
final.value_proposition: A short home CPR or infant CPR practice kit given to families at the moment it matters, with the clinical partner holding the customer relationship.
final.next_action: Run the proposed two-arm test X1 (estimated about 18000 EUR, 12 weeks): trigger-point clinic offer versus open online offer at the same price, plus a funder-paid arm, measuring uptake and completed practice at 8 weeks. Confirm partner access, costs and sample size first, since those are my estimates.
final.uncertainty: High. No sales volumes, prices, margins or uptake data were found for CPR Anytime or any consumer kit. The NICU source reports an American Heart Association kit donation, so it does not show Laerdal's role or revenue. The 2006 NBC piece shows a $30 consumer kit existed but gives no sales. X1.name: Two-channel demand pilot for a home CPR kit
X1.method: Randomised comparison of three offers over 12 weeks in one US region. Arm A: a trigger-linked offer delivered by a partner hospital at discharge from a family-facing unit (T1 pathway). Arm B: an open online offer to households with no trigger, advertised by paid search (tests unprompted individual demand, T2). Arm C: a group offer to employers or schools that buys a 10-person kit (T2 organisational pathway). Track kit take-up and completion of a short training module at 4 weeks.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 300 families in Arm A via 2 partner units, about 2000 ad impressions to generate about 150 households in Arm B, and 3 to 5 organisations in Arm C. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Take-up rate per 100 offers exposed and completion of the training module at 4 weeks, per arm. Also cost per completed trainee per arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A take-up and completion clearly higher than Arm B, because the trigger makes the risk concrete and the institution handles the purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm C yields the most trained people per sale and per euro; Arm B take-up stays low, with cost per completion high in paid search.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm A completion is at least 2 times Arm B completion and Arm A cost per completion is under the price a funder would pay for a discharge programme, keep T1 and scope an institutional pilot. arguments.name: Two-channel demand pilot for a home CPR kit
arguments.method: Randomised comparison of three offers over 12 weeks in one US region. Arm A: a trigger-linked offer delivered by a partner hospital at discharge from a family-facing unit (T1 pathway). Arm B: an open online offer to households with no trigger, advertised by paid search (tests unprompted individual demand, T2). Arm C: a group offer to employers or schools that buys a 10-person kit (T2 organisational pathway). Track kit take-up and completion of a short training module at 4 weeks.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 300 families in Arm A via 2 partner units, about 2000 ad impressions to generate about 150 households in Arm B, and 3 to 5 organisations in Arm C. Estimated, not observed.
arguments.measure: Take-up rate per 100 offers exposed and completion of the training module at 4 weeks, per arm. Also cost per completed trainee per arm.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A take-up and completion clearly higher than Arm B, because the trigger makes the risk concrete and the institution handles the purchase.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm C yields the most trained people per sale and per euro; Arm B take-up stays low, with cost per completion high in paid search.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if Arm A completion is at least 2 times Arm B completion and Arm A cost per completion is under the price a funder would pay for a discharge programme, keep T1 and scope an institutional pilot. If Arm B completion is at least half of Arm A, or Arm C cost per trainee is under half of Arm A, T1 is weakened and T2 becomes the lead. If neither, neither channel justifies a consumer proposition and no expansion is recommended.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a standalone consumer proposition now. Keep the current US home kit as is, and test whether an institution-funded, trigger-linked offer (for example at discharge from a family-facing unit) can give Laerdal a repeatable channel before investing further. If the pilot does not show clear completion gains over open individual offers, the recommendation is no expansion.

position.recommendation: Do not launch a consumer product. If anything, test a contractor-led residential zoning kit in one region for under EUR 15k over 12 weeks, under a decision rule. The existing evidence shows Belimo has sold residential-listed components since 2015 and that Resideo targets contractors first. It shows nothing about homeowner demand or Belimo's residential sales volume, so the consumer case is unproven.

frame.objective: Decide whether Belimo should invest in a differentiated proposition aimed at individual (consumer or homeowner) buyers, beyond its commercial-building HVAC components, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real question is whether any individual buyer will pay for or choose Belimo-branded or Belimo-enabled value at a price and volume that justifies the spend, given that Belimo sells to OEMs, contractors and integrators.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no company contact or internal data
Search budget of 8 searches (7 remaining)
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions
Some financial and contractual detail (channel margins, OEM contracts, pricing) is likely not public
No claim about company intentions can be made from the brief
Must distinguish what Belimo already sells to individual buyers, if anything, from what it might sell
alternatives: A. No expansion: remain a B2B component supplier to OEMs, contractors and integrators; invest in commercial-building growth (e.g. digital services, energy-efficiency software) instead
B. Digital/service layer for commercial buildings sold to building owners or facility managers, a different B2B customer group
C. Residential-retrofit route: sell actuators, valves or sensors to homeowners through DIY, online retail or home-improvement channels for specific use cases such as radiator or heat-pump control
D. Partner-led consumer route: license or white-label Belimo technology to smart-thermostat or heat-pump brands that already own the consumer relationship
E. Installer-led residential route: a homeowner-facing kit sold and installed by heating contractors, with value captured through the installer relationship and a redesigned low-cost product
F. Adjacent-market test: energy metering or indoor-air-quality sensing for small landlords or building occupants, without targeting consumers directly

T1.claim: Homeowners do not choose damper actuators or valves; the heating or HVAC contractor specifies them. So a residential proposition can only earn revenue if it is sold through the contractor, who holds the homeowner relationship and the purchase decision.
T1.who_benefits: Heating and HVAC contractors, who earn installation margin and want reliable, easy-to-specify parts; Belimo, if its components are the default in contractor-specified residential retrofits.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A contractor replacing or upgrading zoning or airflow control in a home already has a trusted reason to specify a known brand, so the homeowner accepts the contractor's recommendation rather than comparing components.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Belimo sells to distributors or contractor supply chains at trade prices, with value captured through component volume and brand preference rather than a homeowner price premium.

Belimo residential-specific SKUs (2015 launch) have contractor distribution
Contractor brand loyalty to components is strong enough to affect specification
predictions: Contractor-facing residential sales grow where contractors are offered a kit with installation support
Homeowner-facing marketing by Belimo generates few leads compared with contractor referral

T1.first_claim: Homeowners do not choose damper actuators or valves; the heating or HVAC contractor specifies them. So a residential proposition can only earn revenue if it is sold through the contractor, who holds the homeowner relationship and the purchase decision.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Homeowners buy comfort and lower bills, and choose the device that delivers them through a familiar interface, so the component inside is invisible and does not drive purchase.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Belimo earns OEM component or licence revenue from the partner's volume, with no need for a Belimo-branded consumer product, consumer channel or homeowner support.

frame.objective: Decide whether Kingspan should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its professional construction customers, and what evidence would justify that investment.

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners wanting lower bills; Kingspan, which keeps the merchant and installer margin
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising energy costs make bill savings salient, and a product sold as a visible DIY upgrade is easier to act on than a contractor-led job requiring a survey and quote
T1.how_value_is_captured: Direct web sales to mainland UK addresses, retaining distributor margin and building a consumer brand and customer data
assumptions: Homeowners can install or pay for installation of rigid board or roll insulation themselves

Direct online channel can serve small orders profitably after delivery costs
predictions: Direct-to-consumer web sales would show repeat growth in enquiries when energy prices rise

T1.first_claim: Homeowners will buy insulation as a self-initiated energy-bill saving if it is sold in a simple, direct, online-led format with clear savings figures, so a manufacturer selling direct to them can capture margin that normally goes to merchants and installers.

T2.claim: Homeowners will not buy insulation on their own initiative because they cannot judge quality or fit, so they need a trusted installer to specify and fit it; a manufacturer that bundles its product with a vetted installer network and a home-survey step can capture the installer's margin and win the job.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners who want assurance and a guaranteed result; the manufacturer, which keeps the job and its recurring installer relationships
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Insulation is hidden, hard to compare and has a poor reputation for shoddy work, so buyers defer to a recommended installer and pay for an assured outcome rather than a box of product
T2.how_value_is_captured: A bundled offer of survey, product and fitting priced as one job, with the manufacturer taking product margin plus a share of installation fees through an accredited installer network
assumptions: Homeowners will pay a premium for a survey and guarantee over buying product alone
Accredited installers will accept the manufacturer's network and leads
Trust, not price, is the main barrier to buying
predictions: Conversion would be higher for a bundled survey-and-fit offer than for product-only online sales
Demand would concentrate in older homes that need deep retrofit, where a survey adds the most value
Customers would ask for installer credentials and guarantees before price
T2.first_claim: Homeowners will not buy insulation on their own initiative because they cannot judge quality or fit, so they need a trusted installer to specify and fit it; a manufacturer that bundles its product with a vetted installer network and a home-survey step can capture the installer's margin and win the job.

assessments.quote: Buyers can access the website and order products with delivery to any mainland UK address.
assessments.does_not_show: Sales volumes, margins, customer numbers or whether the direct channel still operates in 2026. A 2011 trade report shows the channel existed, not that homeowners bought through it or that it was profitable.

assessments.quote: Focus on older homes: the scheme is particularly beneficial for homeowners of older homes (pre 2011) that require more extensive upgrades and deep retrofits.
assessments.does_not_show: Whether the scheme is installer-led or self-serve, whether a survey or guarantee is included, whether homeowners pay a premium for it, or how many homes it has served. It shows that the company targets deep retrofits, which fits T2 but does not test it.

assessments.quote: Only 6.3% of homeowners plan to install insulation in the next 12 months (Ecofurb).
assessments.does_not_show: Whether the 6.3% figure is representative or reliably measured, since it is reported secondhand from Ecofurb. It does not show what share would buy through a bundled installer offer, nor whether direct-to-consumer buyers differ from the general population. Stated intention is also a weak guide to action.

assessments.quote: The NAO report states that nearly all of the faulty installations have been remediated, at a cost of up to £18,000 per property.
assessments.does_not_show: Which installers or products were involved, or whether a survey-and-guarantee bundle would have prevented the failures. It shows that poor retrofit installation is real and costly, which supports the premise that buyers need assurance. It does not show that a manufacturer-linked installer network would be any better, and the excerpt is a trade-press summary of an NAO report I have not read directly.

X1.name: Two-offer landing page test in one UK region
X1.method: A UK landing page for home insulation with two randomised offers: (a) buy the product directly with delivery, and (b) book a survey and fitted installation through an accredited installer. Traffic is bought through paid search and social ads targeting homeowners of pre-2011 houses. Each click is randomly assigned to one offer. Proposed budget EUR 12,000 for ads and EUR 8,000 for page build, tracking and installer partner fees.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 8,000 ad clicks in one region over 8 weeks, roughly 4,000 per arm
X1.measure: Conversion to a paid order or a confirmed survey booking per 1,000 clicks, plus cost per conversion and the share who ask about installer credentials or guarantees

prediction_by_theory.T1: Product-only direct orders convert at least as well as the bundled offer, and cost per order is low enough to be profitable
prediction_by_theory.T2: The bundled survey-and-fit offer converts several times better than product-only, and buyers ask about installer credentials before price

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if the bundled offer gets at least 3 times the conversions of product-only per 1,000 clicks, and the bundled cost per booking is below the proposed EUR 150 margin floor, favour T2 and build a pilot with installers. If product-only converts at least 1 per 1,000 clicks and beats bundled, favour T1. If neither threshold is met, the result is inconclusive and the consumer proposition should not be funded.

final.recommendation: Do not fund a consumer product launch or a direct-to-consumer web business now. Keep the professional construction business as the base case. If leadership wants to test the consumer option, fund only the proposed two-offer landing page test in one UK region, with a bundled survey-and-fit offer and pre-agreed thresholds.
final.target_customer: Homeowners of older (pre-2011) UK or Irish houses needing deep retrofit, if the test confirms demand. Not yet validated.
final.value_proposition: A trusted, assured retrofit: survey, product and fitting through a vetted installer, priced as one job with a guarantee. Not a product-only online sale.
final.next_action: Scope the proposed test (about EUR 20,000 over 10 weeks, all figures analyst-proposed) and agree decision thresholds in advance. Ask the company for internal data on the existing direct channel's sales and margins.
final.uncertainty: Consumer reach is real but unmeasured. Only verified evidence of direct sales is a 2011 UK trade report. The 6.3% intent figure is secondhand. Kingspan consumer pages are company claims with no sales data. Installer economics, channel conflict and non-public financial detail are unknown.
would_change_if: Test shows product-only direct orders at least 1 per 1,000 clicks and beating the bundled offer, favouring T1
Bundled offer fails the proposed 3x conversion over product-only, or cost per booking exceeds the proposed EUR 150 margin floor
Internal data shows the existing direct channel is already large and profitable
Accredited installers refuse manufacturer-linked leads, or merchants retaliate
A representative survey shows far more homeowners planning retrofit than 6.3%

The only proposition worth testing is an installer-mediated, bundled retrofit offer for homeowners of older homes, in one region, with a stop rule. Keep existing professional and merchant channels as the base case.

frame.objective: Decide whether Kingspan should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case, beyond its professional building envelope products, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The aim is to learn whether individual buyers can be reached and would pay a premium, not to prescribe a company action.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or internal data.
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public, so gaps must be stated rather than filled.
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and 12-week maximum are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
8 searches in total (7 remaining); evidence must be gathered selectively.
Current consumer reach (direct-to-consumer sales, retail channels, DIY ranges) is unknown and must be established from sources before theorising.
Any observed number cited must come from a source actually read; proposed test parameters must be labelled as proposed or estimated.
alternatives: A. No consumer expansion: keep serving construction professionals and invest in existing channels.
B. Product redesign for a consumer use case, such as simpler DIY-installable insulation boards for home retrofit sold through existing merchants.
C. New route to buyers with the same product: online retail, builders' merchants or installer networks that reach homeowners.
D. New customer group: self-builders, renovators or homeowners in a specific retrofit segment, for example energy-grant-funded upgrades, with bundled installation and financing.
E. Installer-mediated or partnered proposition: certified installers or an energy-service company own the buyer relationship and Kingspan supplies product or brand.
F. Adjacent service not yet considered: consumer-facing retrofit financing or energy monitoring bundled with insulation, where value may come from the service rather than the panel.

T1.claim: Homeowners buy insulation when a trusted installer and a financing or grant route make the retrofit simple and visible. A branded, installer-mediated retrofit offer, not a DIY panel, would let Kingspan capture a premium because it owns the trust and the bundle.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners of older homes who face high energy bills and grant-scheme eligibility; Kingspan if it supplies the panel and the brand; certified installers who gain leads.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Insulation is a low-visibility, high-disruption purchase with uncertain performance. arguments.objective: Decide whether Kingspan should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for one specific use case (for example home retrofit or self-build), beyond its professional building envelope products, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. position.recommendation: Do not build a standalone consumer brand yet. Laerdal already sells home CPR training kits (CPR Anytime) and mini manikins for groups, so the question is whether to expand the institutional and trigger-timed channel that already exists. Pilot that channel through partner clinics and employers before committing to a direct consumer proposition, and treat the 2006 $30 kit as evidence that individual purchase exists but is not proven at scale.

arguments.name: Trigger versus institutional channel test for home CPR kit demand
arguments.method: Run a time-limited online and clinic-referral offer for a home CPR kit in two arms: one reached through a trigger-timed pathway (new-parent or cardiac-patient content and discharge leaflets, offered through partner clinics) and one reached through a general public and employer channel with no trigger framing. Track uptake and completion of training. Use a small pilot with a partner clinic or patient organisation so buyers are identifiable.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 400 site visitors or referrals across two arms, roughly 200 per arm, over 8 weeks; estimated, to be confirmed with partner
arguments.measure: Kit purchase or free-kit request rate per 100 exposed people, and completion of the online training module within 14 days of purchase

prediction_by_theory.T1: Institutional or trigger-timed channel gives a clearly higher purchase or request rate than the general channel, and most purchases come through partner institutions rather than open web sales
prediction_by_theory.T2: Trigger framing lifts purchase rate among those with a recent trigger, but the general channel also sells to people without a trigger at a non-trivial rate, so the gap is smaller than T1 predicts and most buyers come from open web sales

arguments.decision_rule: Favour T1 if the institutional or trigger-timed arm gives at least 2 times the purchase or request rate of the general arm and at least half of all completed purchases come through partner institutions. Reject T1 if the general arm reaches at least 80 percent of the trigger arm's rate and open web sales make up most purchases. Otherwise treat results as inconclusive and repeat with a larger sample.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not build a standalone consumer brand yet. Laerdal already sells home CPR training kits (CPR Anytime) and mini manikins for groups, so the question is whether to expand the institutional and trigger-timed channel that already exists. Pilot that channel through partner clinics and employers before committing to a direct consumer proposition, and treat the 2006 $30 kit as evidence that individual purchase exists but is not proven at scale.

T1.claim: Consumer household gloves are a retailer- or brand-controlled category where the consumer brand owner captures most value through marketing and shelf access. Ansell's contribution is R&D and manufacturing, and whether that earns a stable margin is contested, so partnering is preferred over owning the consumer proposition only if the partner pays for R&D.
T1.who_benefits: Retailers and consumer brand owners (such as FHCS) who control shelf, marketing and pricing; Ansell as supplier of R&D and manufacturing.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Household glove buyers choose on brand, price and shelf position rather than on protection performance, so a brand owner with consumer research and retail reach wins the sale while the glove maker earns a supply margin.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Supply and R&D fees or manufacturing margin from a partner, with the partner carrying marketing, retail and inventory risk.

It weakens the claim that manufacturing earns a protected margin, but does not show the consumer proposition fails.

X1.name: Task-specific vs generic glove direct-response test
X1.method: Two-arm online direct-response test. Arm A: a generic household glove page at the price of a mass-market pack. Arm B: the same glove, relabelled and framed for one defined cleaning task, with a stated performance claim, at a premium price. Traffic is bought through paid search and social ads for each arm, with equal budgets, and orders are tracked by arm. A short follow-up survey asks buyers which task and which factor drove the purchase.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 800 unique visitors per arm, roughly 2,000 to 2,500 EUR of paid traffic per arm over 6 weeks, with a pilot period of 2 weeks to check tracking. Visitors limited to one country where Ansell has no current consumer retail presence, to avoid cannibalising existing sales.
X1.measure: Conversion rate per visitor, average selling price, and contribution per visitor after product, shipping and ad cost, by arm. Secondary: share of buyers citing the task or the performance claim in the survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A and Arm B convert at similar rates and the premium price in Arm B does not hold; buyers cite price or brand, not the task. Contribution per visitor is similar or lower in Arm B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts at a higher rate or holds the premium price, and buyers cite the task and performance claim. Contribution per visitor in Arm B is clearly higher than in Arm A.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: favour T2 if Arm B contribution per visitor is at least 1.5 times Arm A and at least 40% of Arm B buyers cite the task or claim in the survey. Favour T1 if Arm B contribution per visitor is below 1.1 times Arm A. Anything between is inconclusive and triggers a second, larger test rather than a launch decision.

revisions.reason: The Hartalega source (a rival's 2023 account of rubber glove margins) contradicts the claim that manufacturing earns a protected supply margin. The partnership quote from FHCS is a counterparty statement, so the division of labour is supported only weakly. The claim that retailers and brand owners hold the consumer relationship remains plausible but is not tested.
revisions.new_claim: Consumer household gloves are a retailer- or brand-controlled category where the consumer brand owner captures most value through marketing and shelf access. Ansell's contribution is R&D and manufacturing, and whether that earns a stable margin is contested, so partnering is preferred over owning the consumer proposition only if the partner pays for R&D.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer glove business now. Keep Industrial and Healthcare as the base. If management wants to explore consumers, run the proposed low-cost task-specific direct-response test (about 20,000 EUR, 8 weeks) before any investment. Prefer a partner-led model over an owned consumer brand unless the test shows a clear premium.

final.value_proposition: A task-specific glove with a stated performance claim, if buyers pay a premium for it. Not yet shown.

arguments.name: Task-specific vs generic glove direct-response test
arguments.method: Two-arm online direct-response test. Arm A: a generic household glove page at the price of a mass-market pack. Arm B: the same glove, relabelled and framed for one defined cleaning task, with a stated performance claim, at a premium price. Traffic is bought through paid search and social ads for each arm, with equal budgets, and orders are tracked by arm. A short follow-up survey asks buyers which task and which factor drove the purchase.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 800 unique visitors per arm, roughly 2,000 to 2,500 EUR of paid traffic per arm over 6 weeks, with a pilot period of 2 weeks to check tracking. Visitors limited to one country where Ansell has no current consumer retail presence, to avoid cannibalising existing sales.
arguments.measure: Conversion rate per visitor, average selling price, and contribution per visitor after product, shipping and ad cost, by arm. Secondary: share of buyers citing the task or the performance claim in the survey.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A and Arm B convert at similar rates and the premium price in Arm B does not hold; buyers cite price or brand, not the task. Contribution per visitor is similar or lower in Arm B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B converts at a higher rate or holds the premium price, and buyers cite the task and performance claim. Contribution per visitor in Arm B is clearly higher than in Arm A.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: favour T2 if Arm B contribution per visitor is at least 1.5 times Arm A and at least 40% of Arm B buyers cite the task or claim in the survey. Favour T1 if Arm B contribution per visitor is below 1.1 times Arm A. Anything between is inconclusive and triggers a second, larger test rather than a launch decision.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

frame.objective: Decide whether Ansell should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its industrial and healthcare protective gloves and body protection, and identify what public evidence would justify that investment.
constraints: Outside analyst, public sources only. The company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions.
Financial and contractual detail may be non-public; state gaps explicitly.
Test budget EUR 20,000 and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Search budget: 7 searches remain, plus one challenge search.
Distinguish company assertions from independent evidence of consumer demand.
alternatives: No expansion: stay focused on Industrial and Healthcare B2B.
Product redesign: adapt the existing glove line for a specific household or hobby use case such as gardening, DIY or cleaning.
Different route to buyers: sell existing products to consumers through retail or e-commerce without redesign.
Different customer group: target a professional subgroup not currently served, such as trades, food service or home caregivers.
Licensing or partnership: a consumer brand or retailer carries the proposition while Ansell supplies the material.
Verify first whether Ansell already sells to individual buyers before assuming a gap exists.

T1.claim: Consumer household gloves are a brand-and-retail business, not a protective-materials business. Ansell's material and manufacturing edge does not translate into consumer willingness to pay, so Ansell sold its household brand and exited the retail channel.
T1.who_benefits: Consumer brand owners and retailers (for example FHCS/Freudenberg) who control consumer research, marketing and shelf placement, not the glove manufacturer.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Households choose cleaning gloves on brand, price and shelf presence. Protective performance is a low-salience attribute for most buyers, so a manufacturer's technical advantage gives little pull at the point of purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Value flows through the brand owner's marketing and retail margin. A manufacturer who supplies material or manufacturing captures only a supply margin unless it owns the brand and channel.
assumptions: Ansell's consumer sales were concentrated in a few European and Asian markets (see 2013 disposal scope).
The 2013 sale transferred brand and consumer business, consistent with FHCS citing its strength in consumer research, marketing and sales.
The 2025 exit of retail household gloves was driven partly by the consumer economics above; this is not confirmed in the excerpt.
predictions: Any new consumer proposition from Ansell would need a licensed or partnered brand owner to reach shelf; a self-branded launch would show weak sell-through.
Consumer buyers would rate brand and price above protective specification when choosing a glove for a household task.
Ansell would show no consumer sales growth in its segment reporting after exit.
T1.first_claim: Consumer household gloves are a brand-and-retail business, not a protective-materials business. Ansell's material and manufacturing edge does not translate into consumer willingness to pay, so Ansell sold its household brand and exited the retail channel.

T2.claim: Buyers pay for a glove when a health or safety need makes the protective specification the reason to buy. In that niche a manufacturer with material and certification expertise can earn a premium, because the spec, not the brand or shelf, drives the choice.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers with a specific sensitivity or hazard, such as skin conditions, latex or chemical allergy, who need a verified specification. A manufacturer that holds the certified material and sells through pharmacy or health-condition channels captures the premium.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: When someone has a diagnosed sensitivity, they search by material and certification, not by brand or price, and they accept a higher price for a product that avoids their trigger. Specification becomes the purchase criterion.
T2.how_value_is_captured: The manufacturer keeps the material and certification margin by selling a verified-spec product through channels where the spec is explained, such as pharmacy or patient communities, rather than through general household retail where brand decides.
assumptions: The sensitive segment is large and identifiable enough to reach at a viable cost.
Buyers in this segment will pay a premium for verified specification over general household gloves.
Ansell's existing material and certification capabilities are relevant to these specifications; this is not yet confirmed from its product sources.
predictions: Buyers in a sensitivity segment would choose by stated specification and would pay more for a verified version than for a general glove.
Sales through pharmacy or health-condition channels would hold price better than sales through general household retail.
A test presenting the same glove with and without a verified-spec label would show a higher conversion and price tolerance with the label, in the sensitivity segment only.

X1.name: Spec-label versus brand conversion test in a sensitivity segment
X1.method: Online storefront test (proposed). Show the same glove at the same price under three conditions: a plain generic listing, a listing with a verified-specification label naming the trigger it avoids, and a listing under a partner brand name. Randomise visitors to conditions and measure add-to-cart and price tolerance by stated sensitivity.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 visitors from paid and community channels targeting people who report glove sensitivity, roughly 2,000 per condition. Estimated budget within EUR 20,000.
X1.measure: Add-to-cart rate per condition, and share choosing the higher-priced variant at each of three price points. Pre-registered comparison on sensitivity-segment visitors only.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The spec label gives no lift over the plain listing; the partner-brand condition converts best and holds price better, because brand and channel drive choice.
prediction_by_theory.T2: The spec label lifts add-to-cart and price tolerance over the plain listing in the sensitivity segment, and the gap is larger than the brand effect.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: proceed to a further test only if the spec-label condition beats the plain listing by at least 25% relative on add-to-cart, with the 95% interval excluding zero, and the spec label beats the partner-brand condition on price tolerance. If the partner-brand condition beats the spec label on add-to-cart, favour T1 and pursue licensing rather than a self-branded spec product. If neither holds, drop the consumer proposition.
