X1.name: Specified-tolerance preference test with home bakers and coffee brewers
X1.method: Online choice test with a landing page and paid-social recruitment. Respondents see two identical-looking consumer scales at different price points: one with a stated tolerance and a calibration certificate, one with no stated tolerance. Measure choice share, and offer a real pre-order option on the specified scale at the end. Proposed, not run.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 600 adults who bake or brew coffee at home at least weekly, recruited in two markets (for example the UK and Germany), with a cell of about 300 per arm
X1.measure: Share choosing the specified-tolerance scale at each price premium (for example +0%, +20%, +40% over the unspecified scale); pre-order conversion on the specified scale

prediction_by_theory.T1: A measurable share, roughly 25% or more, chooses the specified-tolerance scale even at a +20% premium, and conversion holds up when the tolerance figure and certificate are shown
prediction_by_theory.T2: Choice share for the specified scale collapses to under 10% once any premium is shown; price dominates and the tolerance figure adds little

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: if at least 25% choose the specified scale at +20% and pre-order conversion is at least 3% of visitors, continue to a consumer prototype test under T1. If under 10% choose it at +20%, drop the consumer line and examine licensing under T2. Between 10% and 25%, treat as inconclusive and do not invest beyond the test.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a Mettler-branded consumer hardware line now. Keep no expansion as the default. Test T1 cheaply before any consumer product spend, and treat licensing or component supply to existing consumer scale makers as the more plausible consumer route, though it is untested.
final.target_customer: No consumer segment is recommended yet. Home bakers and home coffee brewers are the candidate niche to test under T1. Consumer scale makers are the potential licensing partners under T2.
final.value_proposition: Not established. Under T1, a published, verifiable accuracy tolerance with a calibration certificate, at a premium. Under T2, licence or component revenue from a consumer brand that owns the mass channel.
final.next_action: Do not commit product spend. If the company wants evidence, run the proposed specified-tolerance preference test (X1, about 12,000 EUR and 8 weeks, both figures my estimates, not yet run). Its decision rule: at least 25% choosing the specified scale at a +20% premium and at least 3% pre-order conversion supports T1; under 10% supports T2. Separately, establish from non-public or company sources whether Mettler already sells to individual buyers through Ohaus, distributors or online.
final.uncertainty: High. The evidence is thin: one US test-kitchen publication (ATK, whose date shows as 2026-10-07, later than the annual report date, which I could not reconcile), two company claims about professional and educational markets, and no consumer sales data. I found nothing that contradicts T2 after one challenge search, but that search was narrow. I could not find any evidence of consumer willingness to pay for stated accuracy. Mettler's contracts, licence terms and consumer sales figures are not public. Test figures are my proposals, not observations.

position.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer precision-scale proposition now. Keep the company's focus on laboratory, industrial and food-retail instruments, and run the proposed low-cost pre-order test (X1) before any product investment. Revisit only if the test shows a premium for verified accuracy.

frame.objective: Decide whether Mettler-Toledo should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its laboratory, industrial and food retail instruments, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The real objective is to find out whether any consumer demand exists that the company's direct-sales, professional-buyer model could capture profitably, not to pick a product.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or intentions are known
Company sells mainly through its own direct sales force, so consumer reach is unknown and must be checked
Some financial and contractual detail is likely non-public and must be flagged as unfound
Test budget assumed at 20000 EUR and 12 weeks maximum (analyst assumptions, not company figures)
Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining; each source read must be quoted exactly
Consumer-grade products carry different margin, channel and brand-risk profiles from professional instruments
alternatives: A. No expansion: keep focus on laboratory, industrial and food retail precision instruments and build no consumer offer
B. Product redesign: simplify an existing professional balance or scale into a lower-cost model for a home or hobby use case (kitchen, coffee, baking, supplements)
C. Different route to buyers: sell an existing or lightly modified product through e-commerce or retail partners instead of the direct sales force
D. Different customer group in a professional niche not yet served: small food businesses, artisan producers, fitness or sports-nutrition labs
E. Software or service layer (calibration, traceability, connected weighing) sold on existing hardware to test demand without new hardware
F. Licensing or partnering: a consumer appliance maker or retailer carries the technology or brand for royalties, avoiding direct consumer selling

T1.claim: Consumers who bake, brew coffee or log supplements will pay a premium for a scale whose accuracy is verifiable, because they treat small weighing errors as a real cause of failed results. A precision-branded scale can capture that premium through its accuracy reputation.
T1.who_benefits: Serious home bakers, coffee brewers and supplement users who weigh ingredients to a fraction of a gram, and the manufacturer if it can sell at a price above commodity kitchen scales.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Recipes and brew ratios are sensitive to small mass errors, so users who experience inconsistent results attribute them to the scale and will pay for stated, checked accuracy.
T1.how_value_is_captured: A premium-priced consumer scale sold through online and specialist retail, with accuracy certification and calibration as the reason to buy, using the existing precision brand rather than the direct professional sales force.
assumptions: A subset of home users notice and care about errors below 1 gram
Accuracy claims are a purchase criterion for this subset, not just a feature
The price premium over commodity scales covers the cost of a consumer-grade build and retail margin
Mettler's brand carries credibility with this subset
predictions: In a blind comparison of recipes, users of a verified-accuracy scale report fewer failed bakes than users of a commodity scale
Stated purchase intent for a verified-accuracy scale is higher among bakers and coffee brewers than among general households
Willingness to pay a premium of at least 50 percent over a commodity scale appears in a conjoint or price test within this subset
T1.first_claim: Consumers who bake, brew coffee or log supplements will pay a premium for a scale whose accuracy is verifiable, because they treat small weighing errors as a real cause of failed results. A precision-branded scale can capture that premium through its accuracy reputation.

T2.claim: Consumer kitchen scales are bought on price and convenience features, not on accuracy. Buyers rarely check or value precision, so a precision maker gains no premium from its accuracy reputation and would have to compete on cost against low-price commodity scales.
T2.who_benefits: Low-cost consumer electronics makers and retailers who sell on price, features and app connectivity; a precision maker would face a cost disadvantage.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Most cooking tolerates a few grams of error, so accuracy is not a salient decision variable. Buyers choose on display, size, price and design, and specifications are often missing from the box or listing.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Only through a low-cost product sold at volume through mass retail and online marketplaces, which conflicts with a direct-sales, high-margin professional model and would require a different cost base.
assumptions: Most consumers do not verify or pay for accuracy beyond roughly 3 grams
Accuracy specifications rarely influence purchase in mass retail
Price elasticity in the consumer scale segment is high
A precision brand cannot match commodity cost without diluting its professional positioning
predictions: In a shelf or listing test, accuracy specifications raise conversion less than price and display features
Price cuts of 20 percent move consumer purchases far more than accuracy claims do
Most mass-market scale listings state no accuracy specification
T2.first_claim: Consumer kitchen scales are bought on price and convenience features, not on accuracy. Buyers rarely check or value precision, so a precision maker gains no premium from its accuracy reputation and would have to compete on cost against low-price commodity scales.

assessments.quote: A range of ±3 grams is common and acceptable for most cooking, and most consumer-level scales don't specify their accuracy range.
assessments.does_not_show: This is one test-kitchen review for a US audience. It does not measure how many home bakers or coffee brewers value sub-gram accuracy, nor what they would pay. It contradicts only the claim that most cooking needs precision, not the narrower claim about a serious-baker segment.

assessments.quote: most consumer-level scales don't specify their accuracy range.
assessments.does_not_show: This is one US test-kitchen observation that most scales omit an accuracy range. It does not show that buyers ignore accuracy when they choose, nor that price or features drive purchases. Absence of a spec on the listing is not evidence of buyer indifference.

assessments.quote: When weighing small amounts of ingredients such as yeast, salt , or xanthan gum, you need a precision scale that goes to a fraction of a gram, as a deviation of a few tenths of a gram can yield a difference in the finished product.
assessments.does_not_show: A test-kitchen editorial stating that small quantities need fraction-gram precision. It does not show that home bakers actually buy such scales, that they would pay a premium, or that the effect is noticed by ordinary users. It is a claim about recipe sensitivity, not about buyer behaviour.

X1.name: Accuracy-premium landing-page test with home bakers and coffee brewers
X1.method: Randomised online test. Paid social and search ads target home bakers and home coffee brewers in one market. Visitors are randomly shown one of three product pages for the same physical scale: (a) commodity listing at base price with no accuracy claim, (b) same scale at base price with an accuracy claim, (c) verified-accuracy version (fraction-of-a-gram, third-party calibration certificate) at a 50 percent price premium. The pages test a refundable pre-order, so purchase intent is measured without shipping product.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 6,000 unique targeted visitors per arm, roughly 18,000 in total, recruited from baking and coffee interest audiences in one country. Estimated, not observed.
X1.measure: Pre-order conversion rate per visitor for each arm, and share of pre-orders in the premium arm that remain after a 14-day cancellation window. Also a 3-question survey on whether the buyer cares about gram-level accuracy.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The verified-accuracy premium arm converts at least 70 percent as well as the commodity base-price arm, and the accuracy claim lifts conversion over the no-claim arm at the same price. Serious bakers/brewers say accuracy matters in the survey.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Accuracy claims add little conversion at equal price. The premium arm converts well below 70 percent of the base-price commodity arm, and the survey shows accuracy ranks below price and features.

X1.decision_rule: Treat T1 as supported and proceed to a costed product plan only if the premium arm's conversion is at least 70 percent of the commodity base-price arm's conversion, AND the accuracy-claim arm beats the no-claim arm at equal price by a margin that is statistically distinguishable at 95 percent confidence, AND at least 60 percent of premium pre-orders survive the cancellation window. Otherwise treat T2 as favoured and do not invest in a consumer line. These thresholds are proposed, not derived from company data.

final.recommendation: Do not build a differentiated consumer precision-scale proposition now. Keep investment focused on laboratory, industrial and food-retail instruments. Run the proposed low-cost pre-order test (X1) before committing product capital to consumers, and revisit only if it shows a real premium for verified accuracy.
final.target_customer: Only if the test succeeds: a narrow segment of serious home bakers and home coffee brewers who weigh small quantities to a fraction of a gram. Not the general household kitchen market.
final.value_proposition: A verified-accuracy scale with calibration certificate, sold on accuracy rather than on features or price. Unproven: the evidence supports need for precision in some recipes, not that buyers will pay for it.
final.next_action: Run test X1 as proposed (8 weeks, estimated EUR 14,000, within the EUR 20,000 budget) with the decision rule as written. First confirm the company's current consumer-facing presence, which I could not verify from public sources.
final.uncertainty: High. Found: a US test-kitchen review saying most cooking tolerates about ±3 g and most consumer scales omit accuracy specs; a test-kitchen editorial on fraction-gram precision for small quantities; the 2025 annual report on direct-sales channels and Ohaus's lower-cost education focus. Not found: consumer sales data, any Mettler consumer line or channel, margins, segment size, or willingness to pay for accuracy. Sources are single observations or company claims, not surveys.

Evidence the company already sells consumer-grade products indirectly with healthy margins

frame.objective: Decide whether Mettler-Toledo should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home or small-business weighing, such as kitchen, fitness or small-batch food scales), beyond its laboratory, industrial and food-retail precision instruments, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The objective is an evidence-based go/no-go and, if go, the cheapest decisive test.

alternatives: A. No expansion: keep the current B2B focus on laboratory, industrial and food-retail customers and invest in existing channels.

B. Product redesign: adapt an existing balance or scale line (lower price, simpler interface, design changes, or a premium high-accuracy personal product positioned on accuracy and certification) and sell it into food-retail or small-business channels.
C. Different route to buyers: sell existing or adapted products to individuals through retail, e-commerce or marketplaces, rather than the direct sales force.
D. Different customer group in the same use case: target small businesses (cafes, bakeries, small producers, home brewers) that need accurate or certified weighing but are not labs.
E. Licensing or partnering: license the precision measurement technology or brand to a consumer electronics or kitchen-appliance maker, keeping the core business intact.
F. Adjacent service or data play: sell calibration, compliance or connected-weighing software to existing users or new small buyers, rather than a physical consumer product.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Mettler sets a higher price for a model carrying a verified accuracy specification and certification mark, sold through retail or e-commerce listings, using its existing metrology and calibration know-how rather than a new manufacturing base.

Retail partners will display the accuracy claim prominently.

frame.objective: Decide whether Mettler-Toledo should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home or hobby weighing, or fitness and nutrition tracking), and identify the evidence that would justify that investment. The aim is to learn the real demand and value-capture mechanism, not to design a product.

Product redesign: a new consumer-specific product (e.g. kitchen or nutrition scale, or connected fitness-linked weighing) sold under the existing brand
Small-business customer group: serve bakeries, cafes, supplement makers and small labs with a simplified, lower-priced line

Recurring service layer: add calibration, compliance logging or data services to existing instruments, without a consumer product

assumptions: Some consumers will pay materially more for stated accuracy than for convenience or design

T1.first_claim: Home and prosumer buyers (serious home bakers, coffee brewers, supplement hobbyists) value measured accuracy and will pay a premium for a scale that is verifiably precise, so a precision brand can earn above-market prices in a niche consumer segment.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to an owned consumer product yet. Keep option A (no expansion) as the default. Run the proposed stated-accuracy test (X1) at under 20000 EUR, because T1 is the only theory that would justify an owned consumer SKU, and the test is the cheapest way to tell T1 from T2. If T1 fails, use option E (licensing) rather than building a consumer brand. The evidence I read is thin: two US product reviews and two company statements, with no market size or consumer-segment data.

frame.objective: Decide whether Mettler-Toledo should build a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (for example home or hobby weighing, fitness or nutrition tracking, or small food businesses) beyond its existing laboratory, industrial and food-retail precision instruments, and identify what evidence would justify that investment. The question is where value could be captured, not whether the company wants to do it.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; the company has not asked this question and nothing here reflects its intentions.
Test budget 20000 EUR and 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures.
Only 7 searches remain; each must discriminate between theories.
Financial and contractual detail (channel economics, consumer-sales share, segment margins) may be non-public and must be flagged as not found where so.
Must first establish how far the company already reaches individual buyers through retail partners, e-commerce or consumer brands, rather than assume it does not.
Brand, precision reputation and direct sales force are assets; a consumer product would need a different channel and price point.
alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with laboratory, industrial and food-retail precision instruments and invest there.
B. Consumer product via existing retail partners: a differentiated home or fitness scale sold through retailers the company already supplies.
C. Direct-to-consumer e-commerce using the brand and accuracy claim as the differentiator.
D. Professional-consumer niche: small food businesses, bakeries, coffee or home-brewing specialists, sold as premium precision tools.
E. Licensing or co-branding: a consumer-electronics partner builds and sells the product under a Mettler-Toledo accuracy certification, taking royalties.
F. Partial move: a limited pilot of a consumer proposition before committing to a product line, or acquisition of a small consumer-scale brand to gain channel quickly.

T1.claim: Home and hobby buyers (serious bakers, coffee brewers, people tracking nutrition) under-buy precision because most consumer scales state no accuracy; a scale with a published, verified accuracy spec would win a price premium from this group, so Mettler-Toledo's accuracy reputation is the differentiator.
T1.who_benefits: Serious home bakers, home coffee brewers and dieters who lose outcomes to scale error; the manufacturer, which captures a premium price and a brand-led direct channel.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who care about outcomes (e.g. gram-precise recipes, dosing) are unable to tell which consumer scale is accurate, so they pick on price or looks. A visible, verifiable accuracy claim lets them choose on the attribute they care about, and they pay for it.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Price premium on a single consumer SKU sold direct-to-consumer or through a specialist retailer, using the existing accuracy and calibration brand; margin comes from premium pricing rather than volume.
assumptions: Some consumers value spec-level accuracy enough to pay more for it.
Most current consumer scales do not publish accuracy, so the spec is a real differentiator.
The accuracy claim can be made credible and cheap enough to ship at a premium price point.
predictions: In a choice test, buyers shown a stated accuracy of about 0.1 g choose the spec-sheet scale over an equally priced unspecified scale more often than chance.
Willingness to pay for stated accuracy is higher among self-described serious bakers or dosers than among general buyers.
Reviews of a verified-accuracy scale mention accuracy more often than reviews of unspecified scales.
T1.first_claim: Home and hobby buyers (serious bakers, coffee brewers, people tracking nutrition) under-buy precision because most consumer scales state no accuracy; a scale with a published, verified accuracy spec would win a price premium from this group, so Mettler-Toledo's accuracy reputation is the differentiator.

T2.claim: Consumer scale purchase is driven by retail shelf price, reviews and retailer placement rather than by accuracy; a precision-brand consumer product would therefore earn little premium through Mettler-Toledo's own channels and is only worth doing through a licensed retail partner who controls the consumer relationship.
T2.who_benefits: Retailers and consumer-electronics or kitchen-goods brands, which control shelf space, pricing and the consumer relationship; the manufacturer would benefit only as royalty recipient.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shop where the product is on the shelf or at the top of a search result, and compare prices on the same screen; accuracy is rarely tested before purchase, so the brand premium is hard to sustain without the partner's retail presence.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Royalty or licence fee from a retail or consumer-brand partner that owns distribution, marketing and pricing; Mettler-Toledo sells the accuracy certification and component, not the consumer relationship.
assumptions: Consumers rarely verify accuracy before buying, so it does not carry the purchase on its own.
Retail partners will pay for a recognised accuracy certification.
Mettler-Toledo's direct sales model does not extend easily to consumer retail.
predictions: Price-sensitivity of consumer scale purchase is high; a test with an accuracy premium of over 20% loses share to cheaper retail-placed alternatives.
Retail partners ask for a certification or component supply rather than an owned consumer brand.
Consumer scale sales concentrate in a few retail channels and listing decisions dominate volume.
T2.first_claim: Consumer scale purchase is driven by retail shelf price, reviews and retailer placement rather than by accuracy; a precision-brand consumer product would therefore earn little premium through Mettler-Toledo's own channels and is only worth doing through a licensed retail partner who controls the consumer relationship.

assessments.does_not_show: Shows a real need for fractional-gram precision in some baking tasks, which supports the existence of a niche. It does not show that the niche is large, that buyers would pay a premium for a stated accuracy, or that Mettler-Toledo's brand would win it. It is a single review, US only, and it sits uneasily with the other ATK review saying ±3 g is acceptable for most cooking, so the niche is narrow.

X1.name: Stated-accuracy choice test with direct-to-consumer landing page
X1.method: Online randomised choice experiment. Serious home bakers and home coffee brewers are recruited through baking and coffee forums and an online panel, then shown one of two product pages at a price premium: (a) a scale with a published, independently checked accuracy of 0.1 g and a stated repeatability, or (b) an otherwise identical scale with no accuracy spec. Arms are priced at parity and at a 20% premium. Measured as click-through to 'add to basket' and an optional stated willingness-to-pay question. Also a retail-shelf variant with a partner store if one agrees.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 1,200 panel respondents (about 300 per arm) who bake or brew at least weekly, plus a forum-recruited sample for the tail. Estimated cost within 20000 EUR budget for panel, landing pages and a 4-week ad test.
X1.measure: Add-to-basket rate per arm; stated willingness to pay for the accuracy spec; share of respondents who cite accuracy as the reason for choice in free text.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The 0.1 g accuracy arm converts at least as well as the unspecified arm even at a 20% premium, and stated willingness to pay for the spec is positive among bakers and brewers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At a 20% premium the spec arm loses clearly to the unspecified arm; accuracy claims do not offset price, and buyers say they chose on price or reviews.

X1.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: T1 is kept as a live theory only if the spec arm at a 20% premium achieves an add-to-basket rate at least 80% of the unspecified arm at parity and the spec arm's stated premium is positive for at least 40% of serious bakers. If the spec arm at a 20% premium falls below 60% of the unspecified arm's rate, T2 is favoured and a licensing route (option E) is preferred over an owned consumer SKU. In between, the result is inconclusive and the test is repeated with a 10% premium.

revisions.reason: SYN-D is a SIMULATED result about a warehouse label printer and packing errors. It measured nothing about wearers or buyers, so it bears on neither T1 nor T2 and changes nothing; it is not cited. T1 stays open: the accuracy-spec gap is supported by a real review, and the fractional-gram need is real but narrow. Willingness to pay for stated accuracy remains untested.

SYN-D is a SIMULATED result about a warehouse label printer and packing errors. It measured nothing about consumer purchasing, retail channels or price, so it bears on T2 as little as on T1 and changes nothing. T2 stays open: the Ohaus price-led segment and the indirect channel for simpler products are real company statements, but they do not show a consumer or retail route.

Supposing SYN-D were real: a warehouse label printer that reduces packing errors would bear on operational cost, not on whether home bakers or brewers pay for stated accuracy. It would change nothing for T1 or T2. It is not cited in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not build an owned consumer product now. Keep no expansion (option A) as the default. Run the proposed stated-accuracy test (X1, estimated 15000 EUR, 8 weeks) to decide between an owned direct-to-consumer SKU (T1) and a licensing route (E, consistent with T2). The evidence supports only a narrow niche: some baking tasks need fractional-gram precision, but most consumer scales publish no accuracy spec and most everyday cooking tolerances are looser. No market size, consumer-segment or channel data was found.
final.target_customer: Serious home bakers and home coffee brewers who weigh small quantities weekly. Size of this niche is not established and must be tested.
final.value_proposition: A consumer scale with a published, independently checked accuracy of 0.1 g, backed by the company's calibration reputation. Unproven: buyers may not pay for the spec.
final.next_action: Run test X1 (proposed, not yet run): online randomised choice test at parity and a 20% premium, using the decision rule in the proposal. Separately, establish whether any existing retail or consumer partner already sells Mettler-Toledo products to individual buyers, since I did not establish how far the company reaches them.
final.uncertainty: High. Sources read: two US product reviews and two company annual-report statements. One review is dated 2026-10-07, which I have not verified. Not found in public sources: consumer or retail sales share, segment margins, channel economics, and whether the company already sells to consumers through any partner. X1 is a proposal only; no result exists. The simulated result SYN-D was not used as evidence.
would_change_if: X1 shows the spec arm at a 20% premium falls below 60% of the unspecified arm's add-to-basket rate, which would favour T2 and licensing.
Stated willingness to pay for accuracy is not positive for at least 40% of serious bakers and brewers.
Evidence shows the company already has a consumer or retail channel that could carry an accuracy-branded scale at low cost.
Market sizing shows the fractional-gram baking and brewing niche is too small to cover product and certification costs.
Non-public data showed consumer sales are already a material share of revenue through partners, which would change the channel calculation.

arguments.name: Stated-accuracy choice test with direct-to-consumer landing page
arguments.method: Online randomised choice experiment. Serious home bakers and home coffee brewers are recruited through baking and coffee forums and an online panel, then shown one of two product pages at a price premium: (a) a scale with a published, independently checked accuracy of 0.1 g and a stated repeatability, or (b) an otherwise identical scale with no accuracy spec. Arms are priced at parity and at a 20% premium. Measured as click-through to 'add to basket' and an optional stated willingness-to-pay question. Also a retail-shelf variant with a partner store if one agrees.
arguments.sample: Proposed: about 1,200 panel respondents (about 300 per arm) who bake or brew at least weekly, plus a forum-recruited sample for the tail. Estimated cost within 20000 EUR budget for panel, landing pages and a 4-week ad test.
arguments.measure: Add-to-basket rate per arm; stated willingness to pay for the accuracy spec; share of respondents who cite accuracy as the reason for choice in free text.

prediction_by_theory.T1: The 0.1 g accuracy arm converts at least as well as the unspecified arm even at a 20% premium, and stated willingness to pay for the spec is positive among bakers and brewers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At a 20% premium the spec arm loses clearly to the unspecified arm; accuracy claims do not offset price, and buyers say they chose on price or reviews.

arguments.decision_rule: Proposed threshold: T1 is kept as a live theory only if the spec arm at a 20% premium achieves an add-to-basket rate at least 80% of the unspecified arm at parity and the spec arm's stated premium is positive for at least 40% of serious bakers. If the spec arm at a 20% premium falls below 60% of the unspecified arm's rate, T2 is favoured and a licensing route (option E) is preferred over an owned consumer SKU. In between, the result is inconclusive and the test is repeated with a 10% premium.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to an owned consumer product yet. Keep option A (no expansion) as the default. Run the proposed stated-accuracy test (X1) at under 20000 EUR, because T1 is the only theory that would justify an owned consumer SKU, and the test is the cheapest way to tell T1 from T2. If T1 fails, use option E (licensing) rather than building a consumer brand. The evidence I read is thin: two US product reviews and two company statements, with no market size or consumer-segment data.
